title: Milwaukee Brewers Get Good News From MLB After Braves Series Win
description: The Milwaukee Brewers have put the MLB on notice with their latest dose of good news, following their Atlanta Braves series win. The post Milwaukee Brewers Get Good News From MLB After Braves Series Win appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Milwaukee Brewers may have only won two out of three against the Atlanta Braves (thanks to Matt Olsen), but they are still one of the best teams in the league. And now, they have put the entire league on notice with a recent MLB announcement.

Monday, August 24th, 2026, is an off day for the Brewers, but that doesn't mean that news doesn't trickle through.

For the first time in over two months, the Los Angeles Dodgers are no longer the top team on MLB.com's Power Rankings.

For the week of August 23rd, the Brewers have been crowned #1.

The @Brewers overtake the No. 1 spot in the latest Team Power Rankings 👀

(MLB x @PolymarketSport) pic.twitter.com/bHk1wyvzMs

The latest power rankings wrote this about the Brewers being ranked at the top: "The Brewers remain on pace for the first 100-win season in their history. They've actually won 90 games or more 12 times, with seven of those coming in the last 18 years and five coming in the last eight. This is as good as it has ever been for Brewers fans."

The Brewers own an 81-50 record with a .618 winning percentage. That record is good enough for the top of the National League, the NL Central, and the MLB.

(Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images)

Here is how the full MLB Power Rankings shake out, along with their rankings last week in parentheses:

Not only do the Brewers have the top spot in the MLB Power Rankings, but they have proven themselves in many statistical categories up to this point in the 2026 season.

The Brewers rank third in stolen bases (129), third in team batting average (.254), second in on-base percentage (.337), fifth in RBIs (611), and fifth in hits (1123).

All of that while ranking last in home runs with 120.

What makes their achievement even more impressive is that they did it without breaking the bank.

According to Spotrac, the Brewers rank 19th in Tax Payroll with $153,744,534.

With the Brewers being the first team to reach 80 wins in the league, there's no telling just how high they will go this year.

title: Tommy John, longtime MLB pitcher and namesake of baseball's most important surgery, dies at 83
description: Tommy John and Dr. Frank Jobe changed baseball from an operating room in 1974.
fullText:
Tommy John, the namesake and first recipient of baseball's most important surgery, died on Sunday, the New York Yankees announced. He was 83 years old.

John was reported to be entering hospice in early August, two years after he announced a battle with bladder cancer. He took the occasion to pen a goodbye letter to fans and other acquaintances on the day of the New York Yankees' Old-Timers' Day, where he was a frequent participant.

"While his incredible longevity and post-surgery achievements changed the fortunes and trajectory of countless athletes around the world, it also overshadowed his excellence as a pitcher, which included consecutive 20‑win seasons with the Yankees," the team's statement read. "We pause to remember the totality of his legacy — his competitiveness and skill, his penchant for conversation, his kind and gracious nature, and his stature as an athletic and medical pioneer."

Thanks to the surgery, John's career spanned 27 years, appearing for six different teams and racking up 288 wins. Only 25 pitchers in MLB history have more wins, and only two — known steroid user Roger Clemens and dead-ball era star Bobby Mathews — are not enshrined in the National Baseball Hall of Fame.

John remains a notable exclusion from Cooperstown, between his successful career and presence in the operating room that changed baseball.

STATEMENT FROM THE NEW YORK YANKEES:

“The New York Yankees mourn the passing of Tommy John, who was a bedrock of our rotation during his time in pinstripes and a longtime favorite of Yankees fans. While his incredible longevity and post-surgery achievements changed the fortunes… pic.twitter.com/p6ndlBxUTb

Before 1974, a torn UCL was an unrecoverable blow for a pitcher's career, with treatment usually consisting of some combination of rest, painkillers and prayer. That appeared to be John's fate after July 17, 1974, when the Los Angeles Dodgers left-hander felt something pop in his arm during the third inning of a start against the Montreal Expos.

As recalled in a comment documented by the Society for American Baseball Research:

"Right at the point where I put force on the pitch, the point where my arm is back and bent, something happened," he explained. "It felt as if I had left my arm someplace else. It was as if my body continued to go forward and my left arm had just flown out to right field, independent of the rest of me."

The eventual diagnosis was a torn UCL, and the man tasked with treating John was Dodgers team physician Dr. Frank Jobe. As Jobe recalled in "The Arm" by Jeff Passan, his advice to John was straightforward: "We just told him to go home … he was through playing baseball."

John, however, was desperate. He was 31 years old and had been a successful pitcher for the Dodgers, Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Indians across 12 seasons up to that point. He did not want that career to end and pressed Jobe for a possible fix.

Jobe's answer was to use a surgery that had been in use for years, just never on elbows. He would take a tendon from John's right wrist and put it in his left elbow, to replace a UCL that turned out to be fully ruptured. He told John there was a 1% chance it would work, but later admitted to Passan that was to avoid false hope. He was pretty sure it could work.

It worked, and the results speak for themselves. After an arduous rehab process that ate his 1975 season, John returned to the mound and went on to play 14 more seasons in the big leagues. He had 124 wins with his first UCL and 164 with its replacement. One All-Star nod with the first and three the replacement. Zero career Cy Young votes, then two runner-up finishes.

John's penultimate season saw him lead the Yankees in starts with 32 at the age of 45. When he retired in 1989, he had tied Deacon McGuire's modern-era MLB record for seasons played with 26, which was later broken by Nolan Ryan.

There is no procedure in the history of sports medicine that has altered a sport so drastically. Modern baseball and its high-octane arms are unthinkable without Tommy John surgery. Among the 10 pitchers to receive votes for the American League Cy Young Award in 2025, eight have undergone the UCL repair named after its first recipient.

Rather than being a career-ender, news of a torn UCL is now essentially received as if the pitcher has been put in timeout for a year. The expectation is he will come back, though there are unfortunately still a few exceptions due to surgery complications. The risk is so minimized these days that there have been reports of horrendously misguided parents volunteering their young pitchers for a new UCL because they think it means a potential velocity bump.

Jobe, who died in 2014, deserves the lion's share of the credit for what the surgery has done, but it took a pushy patient to get him there.

title: 6 NBA teams screwed over by the schedule release
description: The idea of playing a balanced schedule is a rarity in American professional sports. fullText:
The idea of playing a balanced schedule is a rarity in American professional sports. An NFL team that finishes in first place in their division one year draws other first-place teams on the schedule the next year. NHL calendars lean heavily on divisional matchups and regional rivalries. MLB moved to a more balanced schedule in 2023, reducing the number of division games and increasing interleague play to even things out.

The NBA does not play a balanced schedule, but the biggest factor in an individual team's success often feels like it has more to do with the travel arrangements than who they're playing on a particular night. Trimming the NBA's 82-game regular season schedule always felt like a silver bullet for many of the league's most pressing problems. Until that happens, teams are still jetting around the country every night to try to sell out as many arenas as possible.

The 2026-27 NBA schedule came out this week. Read our take on the league's 10 biggest rivalries for the upcoming season. With a little help from Shamit Dua's NBA Schedule Dash Board, these are the teams who got hit the hardest by the schedule makers this year.

The Celtics' 16 back-to-backs are in a five-way tie for the most in the NBA. They play 22 times in a stretch of three games in four nights, which ranks as the eighth hardest in the league. They are -4 in "net rest" games, which measures who the more tired opponent is in a given game. The Celtics aren't just dealing with the loss of Jaylen Brown this season, they're also needing to navigate one of the league's hardest travel schedules. I still think the Celtics will be a regular season wins machine, and I wouldn't count them out for grabbing the No. 1 seed in the East, but the road to get there looks more daunting after the schedule release.

The Pelicans have the hardest schedule in the NBA this year. New Orleans plays a league-leading 16 back-to-backs, they're the only team in the NBA with 27 'three in four nights' stretches, and they have a -5 net rest disadvantage. The Pelicans already had the league's seventh-lowest over/under at 29.5 wins coming into the season, and it feels like it's going to be an uphill climb to even hit that number. New head coach Jamahl Mosley has his work cut out for him. After years of believing in Zion Williamson, I'm finally giving up the dream that he can be one of the NBA's best players. At this point, I'm more interested in seeing what Jeremiah Fears and Derik Queen can do together.

The Bulls are one of the league-leaders with 15 back-to-backs this season. They play a stretch of three games in four nights 24 times, which is the fourth most in the league. They're -3 on "net rest," which is third-hardest in the league. The Bulls also have five time zone crossings on no rest, which is the fifth-most in the league. The first 15 games of the season are especially brutal for Chicago, with two games against Boston, two games against the Knicks, two games against the Sixers, and one game each vs. San Antonio, Minnesota, and Cleveland. The Bulls are starting yet another rebuild, but it's going to be difficult for this fanbase to be patient when the team has the third worst cumulative record in the NBA after the last nine seasons. This year is more about figuring out if they have a future star in Caleb Wilson, and seeing how Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey develop in their third year together. The Bulls actually have a decent bench led by Leonard Miller, Jalen Smith, and Tre Jones, and they're going to need it with this type of schedule.

The Cavs missed out on LeBron James and got a tough schedule to boot. Cleveland is tied for the league-lead with 16 back-to-backs. They have 23 'three in four nights' games, which is the sixth hardest in the NBA. They're a -2 in rest advantage, also sixth hardest. The Cavs have done a whole lot of nothing this summer coming off the world's least convincing conference finals run, but there's still time to potentially land Peyton Watson or swing a big trade. I just get the sense that Cleveland's Eastern Conference rivals are passing them by … unless Evan Mobley has another leap left in him.

The Mavericks have 16 back-to-backs (tied for the most in the league), and they're at a -3 net rest advantage. It will be fascinating to see how Dallas manages Kyrie Irving as he returns from a torn ACL at age-34. The team will also have to manage Dereck Lively II, because the 22-year-old big man still hasn't been cleared to run after having foot surgery in December. I could see a world where Cooper Flagg takes a big leap and carries the Mavs to playoff contention, but it's important to remember Flagg won't turn 20 years old until just before Christmas. It might be wise for Dallas' new front office to take a more long-term view around their franchise star.

The Lakers play 15 back-to-backs. They face three games in four nights 26 times, which is the second most in the league. There's so much riding on Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves this year. Both of them dealt with injuries last year, playing 115 out of a possible 164 games. That's not going to cut it this year. Doncic and Reaves need to carry this offense every night without LeBron James around, and the Lakers probably don't want to know what happens when Quentin Grimes needs to be their first or second option for a night. Will the Lakers have a plan to save Luka in some back-to-backs? It's going to be a battle in the Western Conference every night, but the Lakers really just need him healthy for the playoffs, unlike last year.

title: Bryce Harper makes request to MLB after Phillies win against Twins
description: Philadelphia Phillies outfielder Bryce Harper offered an idea about the Field of Dreams game.
fullText:
The Philadelphia Phillies and Minnesota Twins faced off Thursday in the 2026 Field of Dreams game in Dyersville, Iowa. The Phillies took the win 7-1, hammering three home runs during the contest.

It was star slugger Kyle Schwarber doing the biggest damage, going 2-for-5 with two home runs and three RBIs. Outfielder Bryce Harper got involved as well, going 1-for-4 with a walk and a fourth inning RBI single.

It was the third Field of Dreams game overall and first since 2022 due to construction in the area. Harper said before the game that he would like the game to be an entire series instead, as reported by Tim Kelly of On Pattinson.

For a whole three-game series to happen at Field of Dreams, there would need to be more permanent housing available in the area. Dyersville is a town of just over 4,300 people and about 70 miles from any interstate highway.

To build more hotels and other lodging would be excellent as far as a potential game/series goes. However, that could end up compromising the charm of the town and game atmosphere.

For now, it is just the one-off game before the teams return to one of their parks to host the rest of the series. The Phillies and Twins will play two more at Target Field in Minneapolis on Saturday night and Sunday afternoon.

MLB wasted no time in scheduling the next Field of Dreams matchup. The Kansas City Royals and Boston Red Sox will square off in Iowa on August 12, 2027.

The star outfielder has appeared in all 123 Phillies games this year, slashing .253/.373/.495 (.868 OPS) with 25 home runs and 72 RBIs. The 33-year-old has remained consistent during his 13-year, $330 million contract.

After Philadelphia's 9-19 start this season, they have managed to climb back in the race. They are currently 65-58, second place in the National League East. They trail the Atlanta Braves by nine games.

The Phillies occupy the third and final NL Wild Card spot for the time being. They will need Harper and Schwarber to get hot as the postseason draws closer in order to make it in.

title: San Francisco to host 2028 MLB All-Star Game
description: San Francisco will host the 2028 Major League All-Star Game, the Midsummer Classic returning to the Giants' Oracle Park 21 years after it hosted in 2007."With its passionate fanbase, world-class ballpark, and rich baseball history, San Francisco will be an outstanding host for All-Star Week, which culminates in one of Major League Baseball's best traditions, the Midsummer Classic," MLB commissioner Rob Manfred said in a statement on Friday.
fullText:
San Francisco will host the 2028 Major League All-Star Game, the Midsummer Classic returning to the Giants' Oracle Park 21 years after it hosted in 2007.

"With its passionate fanbase, world-class ballpark, and rich baseball history, San Francisco will be an outstanding host for All-Star Week, which culminates in one of Major League Baseball's best traditions, the Midsummer Classic," MLB commissioner Rob Manfred said in a statement on Friday.

"We look forward to bringing the excitement of All-Star Week and the celebration of baseball to the Bay Area."

The last time the All-Star Game was held at the waterfront ballpark, Japanese star Ichiro Suzuki was named Most Valuable Player after hitting the first inside-the-park home run in the history of the mid-season exhibition.

The event will mark another major sporting celebration for the Bay Area. The San Francisco 49ers' Levi's Stadium hosted the Super Bowl in February and six World Cup matches last month, and the Golden State Warriors hosted the NBA All-Star Game in February of 2025.

Wrigley Field, venerable home of the Chicago Cubs, is scheduled to host next season's All-Star game.

fullText:
The Philadelphia Phillies are coming off a series loss to the St. Louis Cardinals, but they'll have a quick turnaround Thursday.

They're set to face the Minnesota Twins in the third-ever Field of Dreams Game, which MLB created around the iconic Kevin Costner baseball movie Field of Dreams.

The game will take place in Dyersville, Iowa, at a custom-built ballpark next to the cornfield featured in the 1989 movie.

Ahead of the matchup, MLB allowed each team to add a 27th player to its roster for the game. The Phillies announced their addition just hours before first pitch after releasing their lineup.

Philadelphia added 28-year-old outfielder Kameron Misner from Triple-A Lehigh Valley as its extra player for the game. He'll wear No. 18.

The Phillies have added OF Kameron Misner from Lehigh Valley (AAA) as the additional player for the Field of Dreams game against the Minnesota Twins. He will wear No. 18.

â Philadelphia Phillies (@Phillies) August 13, 2026

The Phillies acquired Misner from the Kansas City Royals less than a month ago in exchange for cash considerations before optioning him to Lehigh Valley. Philadelphia kept him on its 40-man roster by designating outfielder Steward Berroa for assignment.

Misner is a left-handed hitter with major league experience, having appeared in 97 career games across three seasons with the Tampa Bay Rays and Royals.

Misner has struggled since joining the Phillies' minor league system, batting just .195 in 12 games. However, he has put together a solid 2026 Triple-A campaign overall, appearing in 75 games and posting a .900 OPS.

The Phillies selected Misner with the No. 35 overall pick in the 2019 MLB Draft, and he'll give them some added flexibility in the outfield because he can play all three positions.

Misner won't start Thursday's game, and the Phillies will likely send him back to the minors Friday before the team travels to Minnesota.

title: Tarp comes off at Field of Dreams as MLB officials hope rain holds off
description: The rain, for now, has stopped. Whether it stays that way is the question hanging over Major League Baseball’s return to the Field of Dreams.
fullText:
DYERSVILLE — The tarp is off. The rain, for now, has stopped.

Whether it stays that way is the question hanging over Major League Baseball's return to the Field of Dreams.

Around 1 p.m. Thursday, Aug. 13, crews began uncovering the diamond at the Dubuque County ballpark after a soggy morning and early afternoon, the first real break from hours of rain ahead of the Minnesota Twins' 6:30 p.m. CT game against the Philadelphia Phillies.

Workers hauled sandbags from the edges of the tarp before lining up across the outfield and wrapping the massive sheet around a long, black corrugated pipe. A swarm of groundskeepers then spread out with leaf blowers and rakes, clearing puddles and working the dirt beneath a gloomy, gray sky.

An MLB staffer told the Register that the tarp came off so crews could begin rehearsals ahead of the game. There was no assurance the break in the weather would last.

"All fingers are crossed," the staffer said.

A round of showers and thunderstorms moved across most of Iowa on Thursday morning, with heavy rain and strong winds among the concerns. Forecasters expected the most widespread rain earlier in the day and some improvement by early afternoon, although scattered showers could linger.

As of shortly after 1 p.m., the rain had stopped at the Field of Dreams Movie Site. But the hourly forecast still called for rain in Dyersville through much of the afternoon and early evening, including around the scheduled first pitch.

The changing conditions were built into Thursday's preparations.

As the grounds crew worked below, the outfield scoreboard cycled through rehearsal messages for an array of possible weather emergencies. One would instruct fans to seek shelter from lightning. Another would tell fans to return to their vehicles if severe weather delayed the opening of the gates. Other test messages covered a weather delay, an evacuation, a cancellation and a postponement of the game until Friday.

title: Dodgers' Freddie Freeman somehow avoids serious injury in frightening fall into visitors' dugout
description: Freddie Freeman apparently avoided serious injury Wednesday night when the Los Angeles Dodgers' first baseman took a frightening tumble down the stairs and into the visitors' dugout while trying to catch a foul popup in the eighth inning. fullText:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Freddie Freeman apparently avoided serious injury Wednesday night when the Los Angeles Dodgers' first baseman took a frightening tumble down the stairs and into the visitors' dugout while trying to catch a foul popup in the eighth inning.

Freeman isn't sure whether he'll play when the Dodgers begin an important four-game series with the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday, but he's grateful his freefall to the dugout floor wasn't worse.

"I didn't hit my head, so that was the key part there," Freeman said. "I am sore. Kneecaps are sore. Shoulder is sore. Hand sore. Wrist sore. I mean, I fell. (But) I'm in good spirits."

Freeman stayed in the game and finished the top of the eighth, but Tommy Edman pinch hit for him in the bottom of the inning before Los Angeles closed out a 4-2 victory over the Kansas City Royals, its fourth in five games.

The right side of Freeman's body took the punishment, but the 2024 World Series MVP apparently didn't break any bones. He'll wait to see how he feels in the morning before he decides whether to play Thursday night when the back-to-back World Series champion Dodgers welcome Milwaukee in a reamtch of last year's National League Championship Series.

Freeman said he simply miscalculated the location of the dugout railing while he tracked Isaac Collins' foul pop.

"I went to lean, like I was going to lean against the rail to catch the ball — and obviously there was no rail," Freeman said with a smile.

Freeman, who turns 37 in one month, said he was fortunate to fall all the way into the dugout, missing the top flight of stairs entirely. That's because when he landed, his head stuck out into the open space above the second flight of stairs that goes down into the visitors' clubhouse instead of banging on the ground.

"Luckily, I was tall, so I missed everything else," the 6-foot-4 Freeman cracked.

This wasn't Freeman's first fielding misadventure: He said he fell into the seats in Arizona roughly a decade ago while he was with the Atlanta Braves.

The Orange County native and childhood Angels fan also said he still remembers the infamous 1999 opening-day dugout fall by Mo Vaughn, who got hurt on the first play of his first game with the Halos.

The Royals rushed to Freeman's side after the fall, urging him to stay on the ground. Freeman decided to get up anyway, and the Dodgers' training staff rushed across the field to check on him.

"I think that we really dodged a bullet," Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts said. "Very scary visually. For right now, he's in good spirits, which I think is a good sign. Just kind of total body soreness."

SAN DIEGO (AP) — Jackson Merrill hit a tying sacrifice fly in the 11th inning and Luis Campusano followed with a two-out single to bring in Sun-Mung Song from second base as the San Diego Padres beat the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 on Wednesday for a three-game sweep.

The surging Padres have won five straight and 15 of 19 to move into the National League's second wild-card spot ahead of Arizona and Philadelphia.

Gary Sánchez doubled home the go-ahead run for Milwaukee off Adrian Morejon (9-2) in the top of the 11th.

Merrill tied it when his sac fly off Antonio Senzatela (9-4) brought in automatic runner Jake Cronenworth. Song, who pinch ran after Ty France was hit by a pitch, stole second before Campusano punched an opposite-field single to right. Luis Lara's throw home was high, allowing Song to slide in headfirst with the winning run.

The Padres tied the game at 2 with two outs in the eighth when Fernando Tatis Jr. raced around from second base to score on Cronenworth's infield single.

Cronenworth hit a bouncer to first baseman Jake Bauers, who flipped it to reliever Aaron Ashby but he was late covering first and Cronenworth beat him to the bag for an RBI single. Ashby turned toward home but didn't make a throw as Tatis sprinted in with the tying run.

Dustin May pitched brilliantly into the eighth for the Brewers. He allowed one run and four hits, struck out six and walked two. He gave up Xander Bogaerts' homer in the third.

Sánchez, who was with the Padres for part of the 2023 season, homered to left field against Robbie Ray in the second.

Brewers LHP Shane Drohan (6-4, 3.87 ERA) is scheduled to start opposite Dodgers RHP Roki Sasaki (5-5, 4.54) on Thursday in the opener of a four-game series in Los Angeles.

Padres RHP Michael King (7-8, 3.37 ERA) is set to start Friday in the opener of a three-game series at Cleveland, which counters with RHP Gavin Williams (11-6, 3.55).

title: Alex Rodriguez: The Dodgers are ‘great’ for baseball
description: While some fans and media believe the Los Angeles Dodgers are ruining Major League Baseball, Alex Rodriguez appears to be a fan of their spending. fullText:
While some fans and media believe the Los Angeles Dodgers are ruining Major League Baseball, Alex Rodriguez appears to be a fan of their spending.

After admitting he voted in Awful Announcing's 2026 MLB local TV announcer rankings during an appearance on The Michael Kay Show on ESPN New York, the discussion turned to the current state of the Yankees, who have been ravaged by injuries and offensive struggles. And while the Yankees remain favorites to win the American League pennant, Kay asked Rodriguez about their biggest potential hurdle to a World Series.

The rich got richer at the trade deadline, when the Dodgers added two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. It reignited conversations about whether the Dodgers are good for baseball or will end up driving owners to continue their push for a hard salary cap during the current labor negotiations. And after Kay held firm that the Dodgers are good for baseball, Rodriguez agreed.

"I think it's great. You and I both would be hypocrites if we said it's not good when we saw what happened in the '90s here in New York, what happened in '09 when Hal Steinbrenner flexed his financial resources to go out and get CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett and the year before we had Johnny Damon," Rodriguez told Kay.

Rodriguez noted that the key to spending money is not making mistakes, suggesting that the $22 million the Yankees spent on outfielder Trent Grisham may have been a mistake. Similarly, the Dodgers shelled out massive contracts for Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in the offseason, which have yet to pan out.

As a former player, current broadcaster and franchise owner, albeit in the NBA with the Minnesota Timberwolves, Rodriguez is in a unique position to weigh in on the Dodgers. It's hard for Rodriguez to be against the Dodgers flexing their resources considering he signed a groundbreaking 10-year, $252 million contract with the Texas Rangers in 2000 before playing for the Yankees during their peak spending era. It would also be hard for Rodriguez to rant against a salary cap, given that he's an NBA owner with a soft cap.

If the Dodgers win their third World Series in a row after adding Skubal to a star-studded roster highlighted by Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, and Freddie Freeman, the calls for MLB to fix its financial imbalance will grow as they head toward a lockout. But the Dodgers' ability to play the role of the villain also undoubtedly makes the playoffs more compelling, which is why they're still great for baseball.

title: Athletics’ Jacob Wilson Sets Unique MLB Record

fullText:
In just his second full season at the major league level, Athletics shortstop Jacob Wilson is already making MLB history.

On Sunday night, as the Athletics picked up a series win over the Boston Red Sox, Wilson played in his 111th straight game without recording an error. By doing so, he surpassed former Athletic Mike Bordick's 24 year old record for the longest errorless streak by a shortstop in the history of Major League Baseball. Bordick set the record at the age of 36 during the 2002 season while a member of the Baltimore Orioles and finished the season with just a single error.

"[I'm] a little surprised that record got broken," Bordick said on MLB Network Radio. "That young man is picking it out there as an Athletic."

"It's a special day for me, but at the end of the day, we got our first series win in a long time against a great opponent," Wilson told MLB.com's Greg Levinsky.

Ironically, Bordick's sole error in the 2002 season was on April 10, 2002, less than two weeks after Wilson was born on March 30. As for Wilson, his most recent error came more than a calendar year ago. He had a single error on July 6, 2025 against the Athletics' Northern California rival, the San Francisco Giants. It was his eighth error of his rookie season.

During the 2026 season, Wilson has had 81 putouts and 128 assists, along with 28 double plays, yet has been perfect to this point.

Wilson, 24, has been limited to just 76 of the Athletics' 118 games this year due to injury, but when in the lineup, he's been one of their  most reliable bats as well. His .269 batting average is the most among any Athletic to appear in more than 70 games to this point in the season and the second-highest amongst any player to appear in more than 20 games, trailing just Zack Gelof's .273 average.

It's been a big year for Wilson, both on and off of the field, as he signed a huge contract extension to stay with the Athletics back in February. His new contract runs through the 2032 season and is worth a total of $70 million. The Athletics also have a team option for the 2033 season, which they'll likely pick up if he continues to develop at this pace.

Wilson has almost certainly entered himself into the conversation for a Gold Glove this season, the only thing holding him back will likely be his low number of games played when the season draws to a close. He'll have to play every inning for the rest of the month to hit the 750 threshold before the Athletics' 138th game to qualify for the award, which may be a tough task.

Wilson has come quite a long way from when the Athletics drafted him sixth overall just three years ago. When healthy, he's been a major bright spot for a struggling team. However, for him to truly show his long-term value to the organization, he'll have to find a way to be on the field more regularly.

title: Hagen Smith, Colson Montgomery Lead White Sox to Series Win Over Guardians
description: Hagen Smith delivered two scoreless innings in his MLB debut, while Colson Montgomery’s three-run homer lifted the White Sox to a crucial series win.
fullText:
It will be the division games that matter most for the Chicago White Sox down the stretch of the 2026 season. And after suffering another difficult-to-stomach sweep at the hands of the Boston Red Sox, the White Sox answered with a big weekend series win over the Cleveland Guardians.

It all came down to Sunday's rubber match, when Davis Martin took the ball and surrendered two runs in the first inning before being removed from the game following a rain delay that lasted more than two hours.

The early stages of the game did not set up well for Chicago. While the offense jumped on Joey Cantillo with three consecutive hits to start the game, the White Sox left two runners in scoring position with nobody out in the bottom of the first inning. They then immediately went into the rain delay trailing 2-1, knowing their starting pitcher would be done for the day after recording just three outs.

That was a big blow for a White Sox team with an already taxed bullpen, one that had been pushed to the limit Thursday night in Boston during a 13-inning defeat. But with a key off day coming Monday, manager Will Venable emptied the tank, and the White Sox relievers proved up to the task. That included left-handed pitcher Hagen Smith, the No. 2 prospect in the White Sox organization, who made his MLB debut Sunday.

Smith's debut was true to form. He recorded his first MLB strikeout on three pitches against Brayan Rocchio, the first batter he faced. He struck out the side in his first inning of work, even managing to punch out the notoriously stingy Steven Kwan.

Smith's second inning, however, was much tougher. He walked three batters to load the bases with two outs, then worked a full count against Rocchio before inducing a lineout to third baseman Miguel Vargas. Smith escaped the jam despite issuing four walks on the day, ultimately throwing two scoreless innings and earning the win in his first MLB appearance.

He got that win thanks to Colson Montgomery, who stepped up with two runners on and two outs in the bottom of the third inning and pummeled a Craig Yoho pitch 110.7 mph for his 26th home run of the year. That blast put the White Sox on top 5-2, a lead they held for the rest of the afternoon.

The Colson Montgomery haters are in SHAMBLES!#WhiteSox lead 5-2 on his 26th home run. pic.twitter.com/zz9rq3tqqt

It was an impressive display by the White Sox, who picked themselves up off the mat following a rough start to the game. Both the offense and the pitching staff did enough to secure the win.

"We all stayed pretty much locked in," Montgomery said of the rain delay during his postgame interview with Brooke Fletcher. "We treated it like a whole new ballgame, 0-0."

That win gives the White Sox their largest division lead of the season. It also put a new team in Chicago's rearview mirror. The White Sox now hold a 3.5 game lead in the AL Central, and it is the red-hot Detroit Tigers who sit in second place, with Cleveland and Minnesota both 4.0 games back.

The Tigers are 7-2 over their last nine games. It's an ironic time for a hot streak after they traded both Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize at the MLB trade deadline, but they are by no means out of the race. The White Sox will have to keep taking care of business and stacking series wins if they want to run away with the AL Central crown.

A series win over the Guardians was a good start, but the difficult tests are not over. Next weekend, the White Sox will travel to Detroit for a three-game series against the Tigers.

Furthermore, Kimbrel's 440 saves are the fifth-most all-time. His 2.67 ERA and 1,314/362 K/BB ratio will only bolster his case as well.

However, the past few seasons have been a struggle for the reliever as he has tried to find a long-term home. He put up a 5.33 ERA in 2024 over 57 appearances in 2024 and only saw 11 major league innings in 2025. During the 2026 campaign, splitting time between the New York Mets and Tampa Bay Rays, Kimbrel has registered a 4.81 ERA and a 32/16 K/BB ratio over his 33 outings.

At 49-70, the Royals aren't competing for a playoff spot, meaning the pressure will be off Kimbrel to immediately come in and be a true difference maker. But at the same time, if the legendary relief pitcher can find his footing, maybe Kansas City is the landing spot he has been looking for all along.

fullText:
The Athletics have parted ways with former general manager David Forst after a season in which the team has struggled to win games.

With a 45-70 record this season, the Athletics have been one of the biggest disappointments in all of MLB. Armed with a load of young, talented, and controllable players, things have seemingly fallen apart for the Athletics, who were supposed to contend for the playoffs this season. Instead, the team is battling the Los Angeles Angels for last place in the American League West, and it cost Forst his job.

The Athletics confirmed in a statement that they have parted ways with Forst, with assistant general manager Dan Feinstein taking over on an interim basis for the rest of 2026.

"David has been an integral part of the A's and our success for nearly three decades. His leadership, dedication, and commitment to this team have helped shape our baseball operations department and position us for the future. We are grateful for everything David has done for our organization," said A's owner and managing partner John Fisher in a statement posted on the team's website.

Forst also spoke after leaving the team that he has spent the last 27 years with, offering a classy statement after exiting the organization.

"It was truly an honor to spend the last 27 years with the A's, especially the last 11 as the GM. This organization is full of incredibly talented, devoted, and good people, and I am lucky to have worked alongside them for so long," Forst said.

The 50-year-old Forst was first hired by the A's in 2000, when he worked as a scout for the team. He then became the team's assistant general manager to Billy Beane in 2004 and was then promoted to general manager in 2015 after Beane left his post.

The Athletics won the AL West just once during Forst's 10 seasons as the team's GM, in 2020, and only made the playoffs three times.

With the team slated to move to Las Vegas for 2028, they will have a new front office in place.

Jefry Yan waited a long time for this moment, and he made sure to enjoy every second of it. The Mets reliever recorded the first strikeout of his major league career Wednesday night against the Cleveland Guardians, freezing pinch hitter Angel Martinez on an 88.7 mph slider in the sixth inning of New York's eventual 6-5 win.

Asked afterward to grade the execution of his signature celebration, Yan did not hold back.

"I went out there to attack him. Once I had him at two strikes, I said, you know what, I'm going to throw that slider," Yan said. "And if I freeze him, which is exactly what I did, I celebrated accordingly."

The celebration itself lived up to the hype that had followed Yan for years. He leaped high into the air with his feet spread apart, landed on the front of the mound, slapped the grass with his left hand, and briefly dropped to a knee before rising with both arms raised overhead. Cleveland fans booed him off the mound, a reaction Yan said did not bother him in the slightest.

Yan's path to this moment took over a decade. Originally signed by the Los Angeles Angels out of the Dominican Republic in 2014, he spent years bouncing around the minors, including a stretch working as a roofer in Arizona to make ends meet, before a stint in Japan and later Colorado's system.

He signed a minor league deal with the Mets last August and was called up from Triple-A Syracuse on Monday, finally debuting at age 29 with the same electric celebration that had already made him a viral sensation in spring training.

title: MLB Trade Grades: A’s Have Quiet Trade Deadline
description: Should the team have done more?
fullText:
While nearly every other MLB team made moves at the 2026 MLB trade deadline to boost its present and future, the Athletics sat on the sidelines, unwilling to shake up a roster that is staring down a fifth straight losing season.

Entering the deadline, it felt like the A's were not going to do much, as the organization continues building in anticipation of its 2028 relocation to Las Vegas. As such, it made sense that the team kept recently extended starters Jacob Wilson and Tyler Soderstrom off the market, as well as promising rookies Henry Bolte, Gage Jump and Joshua Kuroda-Grauer.

The reason why the team did basically nothing was that it had no healthy, valuable players to put on the trade block. Injuries and performance regression were major factors behind the team's collapse over the past couple of months.

The A's two pending free-agents, left-handed pitcher Jeffrey Springs and second baseman Jeff McNeil, stayed with the team. Their poor performances and team-options for next season likely discouraged contending teams from pursuing them.

The Athletics' lone move was announced right at the deadline. The club traded 25-year-old outfielder Colby Thomas to the Philadelphia Phillies in exchange for right-handed reliever Seth Johnson.

Thomas had plenty of opportunity to prove himself with the Athletics since he made his MLB debut last August, but he failed to provide much of an impact. With the A's, he accumulated 10 home runs and 30 RBIs over his first 234 major league at-bats. Now he goes to Philadelphia, where he will look to provide some thump against left-handed pitchers for a Phillies team in the postseason hunt.

Johnson can immediately slot into an A's bullpen in need of help. Through 16 appearances with the Phillies this season, the hard-throwing 27-year-old recorded a 1-0 record, a 5.51 ERA and 20 strikeouts. He has fared significantly better at Triple-A, going 1-1 with a 2.17 ERA at that lower level.

They traded from a position of strength, getting rid of Thomas, who projects as only a platoon bat due to the incompetence he has shown against right-handed pitchers. In return, they acquired a former highly ranked pitching prospect who could help a bullpen that owns the worst ERA in the majors

Johnson's electric arsenal consists of a high-90s four-seam fastball and a power slider. He has struggled to limit the walks, making him a natural fit for this walk-happy pitching staff. If the A's can harness his stuff and help him throw more strikes, he could emerge as a late-inning weapon for this bullpen-needy club.

The Green and Gold could have made more of an impact had starting catcher Shea Langeliers not suffered a torn meniscus. Given his multiple years of team control and elite all-around performance, Langeliers would have fetched the Athletics a return on par if not bigger than what the Boston Red Sox sent to the Baltimore Orioles in exchange for mutli-time All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman.

Unfortunately, Langeliers' potential season-ending injury took him off the market. It also likely contributed to the team keeping fellow catcher Jonah Heim, a free-agent at season's end.

title: MLB trade deadline winners and losers: Dodgers, Cubs and Padres all go big, while the Mets sell nearly a third of their roster
description: The Los Angeles Dodgers now have Tarik Skubal. The Boston Red Sox now have Adley Rutschman. The New York Mets now have a fully open calendar for October.
fullText:
Another MLB trade deadline has come and gone, with every contender in MLB making some sort of addition at the expense of the teams embracing reality.

It will be a long time before we understand the full ramifications of these trades due to the volatility of prospects, but no day on the MLB calendar shows which way the wind is blowing more than deadline day.

The Los Angeles Dodgers now have Tarik Skubal. The Boston Red Sox now have Adley Rutschman. The New York Mets now have a fully open calendar for October.

Let's dive into what all of this means, starting with the team that will be the talk of baseball well beyond the 2026 season.

If the Detroit Tigers were going to admit defeat and trade Tarik Skubal, the Dodgers loomed as the inevitable destination. And not for a boorish "The Dodgers get EVERYBODY!" reason.

There were basically four, maybe five teams good enough this season to justify giving up the price of two top-100 prospects and more that the Dodgers paid: the Dodgers, the Milwaukee Brewers, the Atlanta Braves, the Tampa Bay Rays and maybe the New York Yankees or Red Sox. Of that group, only the Dodgers, Brewers and Rays really had the prospect depth to make the deal happen.

The thing is, though, the Brewers and Rays usually need those prospects in a way the Dodgers don't. Those teams build their contenders via affordable pre-arb and arbitration talent, with free agency as an occasional indulgence. Meanwhile, Zyhir Hope, the crown jewel of the Dodgers' prospect package was — and we're not joking here — the third-best outfielder on L.A.'s Double-A team, according to most prospect rankings, behind Josue De Paula and Mike Sirota.

All of that left the Dodgers without another legitimate suitor to compete against. They paid a completely reasonable (but still considerable for a rental) price, Hope and two high-risk, high-reward pitchers in River Ryan and Brady Smith, in exchange for maybe the one guy available at the deadline who could have meaningfully improved their World Series odds.

They didn't stop there, either. Despite a comically large rotation depth chart, especially with Eric Lauer and Emmet Sheehan not being traded, L.A. still went for Royals starter Kris Bubic, a 2025 All-Star who is currently on the injured list but could be useful down the line.

And with Will Smith and Dalton Rushing both now on the injured list, the Dodgers brought in familiar faces Ben Rortvedt and Hunter Feduccia, who can at least offer an improvement on their worst-case scenario at the position.

No organization in all of sports combines resources, competence and the urge to bathe in the blood of your enemies quite like Andrew Friedman's front office. It was no different at this year's trade deadline.

The Dodgers might have made the biggest splash, but the crown for most total value added at this year's deadline belongs to the Cubs, who overhauled a rotation that badly need overhauling.

The team had already acquired David Peterson from the New York Mets, and the left-hander has been more than solid outside of a bizarre meltdown early last month. Then they got Kevin Gasuman from the Toronto Blue Jays, Clay Holmes from the New York Mets and Braxton Garrett from the Miami Marlins.

Gausman should offer instant impact. Holmes was the Mets' most reliable starting pitcher before he fractured his right fibula in May, but his return from the injured list is imminent. Garrett has looked promising in the past, though he's still trying to find his footing after undergoing internal brace surgery in 2024.

Chicago also landed reliever Ryan Zeferjahn from the Los Angeles Angels and outfielder Tyrone Taylor from the Mets, filling two other notable needs.

This team is definitely better than it was a couple of days ago, and it wasn't cheap, with top-100 prospects Jefferson Rojas and Moisés Ballesteros among the several prospects leaving the organization. It probably won't be enough to nullify the Brewers' 6.5-game lead in the NL Central, but this squad suddenly looks like by far the best wild-card team in the NL.

Never change, A.J. Preller. We really do mean that.

For the past few years, the San Diego Padres have been seeing the bill come due. They once had one of the most enviable collections of young talent in baseball (maybe the most enviable other than their neighbors to the slight north), but that has deteriorated through a series of win-now trades.

Now, the Padres sit at 58-54 entering play Monday, which is a vast improvement on where they were 10 games ago, and they're one game out of a competitive wild-card race. They have a minus-12 run differential. Their high-priced core is visibly aging.

So, of course, they bought again.

This time, San Diego improved a bad rotation by bringing in Robbie Ray from the San Francisco Giants and Casey Mize from the Detroit Tigers, sending away the No. 2, 4 and 9 prospects in a weak system, according to MLB Pipeline.

The Padres will remain competitive this season. They will have more questions to answer in the offseason, when top starter Michael King likely opts out and Ray and Adrian Morejon hit free agency.

That's for future Preller — or, and we say this ominously, someone else — to figure out.

It's refreshing to see a Pirates team try, even from 3.5 games out of the last wild-card spot entering Monday.

Pittsburgh ranks second in MLB in runs scored and seventh in runs allowed. There's enough talent in the rotation that the bullpen was clearly the place for improvement, and improve they did.

In deals for Luke Weaver from the Mets, Kirby Yates from the Angels and Lake Bachar from the Marlins, the Pirates bought as hard in the bullpen as any team at the deadline this year.

This is still a team with holes, and one that definitely needs to pray Paul Skenes' recent velocity issues are a temporary nuisance. And yet, this is now Pittsburgh's best chance in years to end a decade-plus playoff drought.

Remember when we said there were four or five teams good enough to have reason to acquire Skubal? Let's go through what those teams did.

The Dodgers obviously did a lot. The Brewers added rotation help with Dustin May and bullpen help with Antonio Senzatela and JoJo Romero. The Rays added a much-needed catcher in Liam Hicks and a classic reclamation project in former All-Star starter Freddy Peralta. The Yankees got some real bats in Luis Garcia Jr. and Heliot Ramos. The Boston Red Sox went for it with the Rutschman blockbuster (more on that later).

The Braves, meanwhile, have a haul headlined by fourth outfielder Lane Thomas. They got a salary dump in Tyler Mahle and minor-league depth in Bailey Falter. They got Brent Suter and Tyler Uberstine, relievers who hardly scream "confident innings in October."

The Braves overall have been excellent this season. Only the Dodgers have better odds to win their division than Atlanta. But, uh, what's the plan once you're facing the Dodgers and their gatling gun of multi-million-dollar arms?

The answer to that can't be "well, the Dodgers are going to win anyway," like some fans will say. Fire any executive who says that. Success is fleeting in MLB, and you can't treat a 100% playoff team like a bonsai tree, making only the most delicate of tweaks, while all the other heavy hitters slam the buy button.

Atlanta obviously isn't done for, but there's no way to describe this deadline as anything better than a disappointment for president of baseball operations Alex Anthopolous.

The Red Sox are going for it! It is legitimately thrilling to see a team go from dead in the water to one of the deadline's biggest buyers, even if Boston's second-biggest acquisition, infielder Curtis Mead, immediately fractured his wrist.

But let's talk about that Rutschman deal.

Rutschman isn't quite the superstar he looked like he would be when he first reached MLB, but he's still one of the game's better catchers and under team control for 2027 too. Boston is probably going to love him.

As for the price general manager Craig Breslow paid for him, let's go to a talent evaluator quoted by Sean McAdam of MassLive.com: "I'm absolutely dumbfounded by this...This is literally one of the most ridiculous trades I've seen in 30 years."

In exchange for a season and a half of their new catcher plus another catcher in Jake Rogers, Boston sent away pitching prospect Anthony Eyanson (their No. 2 prospect at MLB Pipelin), pitching prospect Kyson Witherspoon (No. 4), outfield prospect Enddy Azocar (No. 5), current back-up catcher Carlos Narváez and a player to be named later.

The baseball world is prone to overrating the value of prospects, but that's still a considerable price for a guy whose median outcome is a quality starter and not much more.

Yes, we just talked about what a haul the Orioles got for Rutschman. It was a good deal, but also one that showed all the bad building up under the supposed mastermind in Baltimore.

Remember 2023? The Orioles won 101 games, they still had the best farm system in baseball, they were about to get a new owner in David Rubenstein who was supposedly willing to spend in a way the Angelos family never did. And at the center of it all was Mike Elias, the former Astros player development lead who was demonstrating the power of alchemy in Baltimore.

What happened next might be the most stark example of a would-be contender failing to take a step forward in recent memory. The Orioles never had the pitching to back up their enviable collection of hitting talent, and then all that hitting talent collectively took a step backward. They went from 101 wins in 2023 to 91 in 2024 to 75 in 2025. They are on pace for 78 wins in 2026, with a farm system that was middling before that infusion of talent from Boston.

The Rutschman trade represents the final stretch of a cycle. Elias appeared incredibly adept at the first part of the cycle, building up talent without having to care about the results on the field. He proved disastrous at the next leg, waiting for a contender to assemble itself in front of him. And now he's sending away the vanguard of that first wave of talent for fuel for the next lap.

There is little evidence the next ride will be any different, but at least Elias is doing what he loves again.

Moving back to the Dodgers, not everyone in that building will have reason to be pleased with what they've done.

Consider the case of Justin Wrobleski, who has been a pleasant surprise in his first year as an MLB starting pitcher. He entered Monday ranked 11th in MLB in ERA while ranking behind only Yoshinobu Yamamoto in innings pitched for the Dodgers. He made his first-team All-Star team last month, and would be one of the most valuable components of nearly any other MLB organization.

He is also likely to be pitching out of the bullpen this postseason if everyone is healthy. As is Roki Sasaki, who is suddenly fulfilling his potential as one of the most-hyped pitching prospects in MLB history. The Dodgers are undefeated in nine appearances by Lauer and he is one injured list return from falling out of this rotation. Sheehan got optioned like 10 minutes after the trade deadline.

In an organization with Skubal, Yamamoto, Shohei Ohtani, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, it's not enough to be good for a season. We're just not sure how any young pitcher is supposed to accomplish more than that in this monstrosity of an organization.

We didn't really expect anything different, but the New York Mets have officially pulled the plug on the most disappointing season in MLB.

With Holmes, Peralta, Taylor, Weaver, Huascar Brazobán, Brooks Raley, A.J. Minter and Rortvedt, the Mets traded away eight players over the past two days. That is 31% of an MLB roster. They got back some decent talent overall, but that's not the win they wanted this season.

It's not a full rebuild in New York, but it's at the very least a moment for reflection. This team was supposed to be Dodgers East with David Stearns running the show with a near-unlimited checkbook, but little has gone right since their magical playoff run in 2024.

title: Best pitching rotations in MLB: Where Dodgers' group led by Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto ranks
description: Here's the rundown on which MLB teams have the best starting pitching rooms with the latest Skubal trade.
fullText:

After the Los Angeles Dodgers finally landed Tarik Skubal following more than a year of trade rumors, the rest of Major League Baseball was put on notice as the league's best team added one of its best pitchers.

The Dodgers now have as many combined Cy Young and MVP awards on their roster (10) as the rest of the National League combined. However, Los Angeles isn't the only team with an elite starting rotation.

Four other clubs rank among the top five starting pitching staffs in baseball, while several strong rotations just missed the cut.

Here's a look at the MLB teams with the best starting rotations following the Skubal trade.

MORE: Tracking news and rumors from the 2026 MLB trade deadline

When at full strength, no team comes close to matching this Dodger lineup 1 through 5. For most teams around the MLB, any one of these pitchers would be their ace. With Snell and Glasnow still on the IL, the Los Angeles pecking order has featured Emmet Sheehan and Roki Sasaki, along with the occasional bullpen game.

Prior to Skubal's arrival on the team, the Dodgers had the league's fourth-best team ERA at 3.60, according to ESPN. Hitters bat on average .216 against the Los Angeles entourage, which is the MLB's lowest mark, along with only 414 total runs against (2nd). Just hours before the MLB trade deadline hit the final bell, the Dodgers traded for Kansas City Royals starting pitcher Kris Bubic, who is still on the IL with a left elbow injury. With yet another deep playoff run looking imminent in the City of Angels, their pitching is a key reason why. Anything other than a World Series trophy hoist for the third year in a row would be a colossal failure for this group.

MORE:Full details of Dodgers' trade for Tarik Skubal

Coming in at the second spot in the MLB's best starting pitching lineups is the New York Yankees. While outfielder Aaron Judge has the biggest name in the Yankee organization, their pitching room is among baseball's best. The AL powerhouse has a league-low 3.30 cumulative ERA, along with the third-lowest opponent batting average of .225.

Since returning from Tommy John Surgery, Gerrit Cole picked up right where he left off. In his last seven starts, the right-handed flamethrower has pitched at least five innings and notched five or more strikeouts. In front of him stand Max Fried and young phenom Cam Schlittler. The Yankees are widely thought to be the American League's top contender despite currently sitting 3.5 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays for the AL East's No. 1 spot.

MORE: Who did the Yankees trade for IF Luis Garcia Jr.?

While the Brewers seem to fall short every year despite a stellar regular season, they've consistently had a strong group of starting pitchers to put them in contention. This year, Jacob Misiorowski has put his name on a pedestal as one of the sport's top arms. The 24-year-old currently tops the MLB charts with 190 strikeouts through 21 games (nine per game), along with throwing a large portion of the fastest pitches in the modern era.

Brandon Woodruff has again fallen victim to injuries, with his latest being a season-ending shoulder surgery. Kyle Harrison is set to return soon after a stint on the 15-day IL with left forearm tightness. Logan Henderson and Brandon Sproat, a young pitcher who was landed in the Freddy Peralta trade with the New York Mets, round out a fine lineup that has a high likelihood of propelling the Brew Crew to another deep postseason run.

While the Tampa Bay Rays have been without Ryan Pepiot for the duration of the 2026 season, Shane McClanahan has picked up another injury after missing the entire 2024 and 2025 campaigns with Tommy John surgery and another elbow procedure. Regardless, Drew Rasmussen and Nick Martinez have held down the fort before the team added Freddy Peralta in a trade with the Mets.

While Griffin Jax was one of Team USA's brightest spots at this year's World Baseball Classic, the 31-year-old struggled to begin this season as a bullpen option. He was eventually moved into one of the team's starting positions and has since recovered well. In his last four outings, Jax has gone more than five innings and recorded six or more strikeouts. Tampa Bay currently boasts the sixth-lowest ERA across the majors (3.68), along with the fourth-lowest opponent batting average (.228).

MORE: Grading the Tarik Skubal trade

Rounding out the MLB's top pitching staffs is the Boston Red Sox. Despite Garrett Crochet being on the IL since April 29 with left shoulder inflammation and still not having a throwing timetable, the Red Sox have ranked quite well in pitching statistics for the 2026 season. Boston currently has the third-lowest team ERA in the MLB (3.53), along with a league-low 410 runs allowed.

Outside of Crochet's misfortunes, Sonny Gray has been nothing short of stellar this season. The journeyman has rekindled the potential from his early MLB career and has tallied a 13-2 record as of August 2, second only to Philadelphia Phillies ace Cristopher Sanchez. Behind Gray stands offseason acquisition Ranger Suarez, who has had an up-and-down 2026 season (4-3, 3.15 ERA, 105 K's), and the young duo of Payton Tolle (6-6, 3.30 ERA, 110 K's) and Jake Bennett (6-4, 2.74 ERA, 46 K's).

title: MLB trade deadline: Giants trade 2B Luis Arraez to Phillies
description: Arraez, who signed a one-year deal with San Francisco last offseason, has bounced back with one of the best batting averages in baseball.
fullText:
Luis Arraez has found a new home, with the San Francisco Giants trading the infielder to the Philadelphia Phillies on MLB trade deadline day, according to ESPN's Jeff Passan. Right-hander Kaleb Kilian is also part of the deal. The Giants' return includes the Phillies' No. 4 prospect per MLB Pipeline, RHP Ramon Marquez, and RHP Marty Gair, according to MLB.com's Mark Feinsand.

Arraez signed a one-year, $12 million deal with San Francisco in January after a surprisingly weak free agency this offseason. But Arraez has done well with the Giants, and his production has ticked back up this season, making him one of the likely players to get dealt ahead of the deadline.

After a middling year with the San Diego Padres in 2025, Arraez is on track for a career-best season coming out of the All-Star break. Though the infielder is sometimes criticized for not having a lot of power on offense, his batting average is one of the best in baseball.

Arraez also has value as a defender, starting at second base with the Giants after being shunted to first base last year with the Padres.

The Giants are one of the bleakest teams in the league this season. Though they don't have the worst record in MLB — that honor is being passed between the Colorado Rockies and the Los Angeles Angels — San Francisco is down near the bottom, and doesn't have a lot of direction.

Arraez has been the sole bright spot for the Giants on an otherwise mediocre team. Unfortunately for fans, that meant he was the best asset for general manager Buster Posey to trade away as San Francisco looks ahead to next season.

title: Blue Jays reportedly trade Kevin Gausman to Cubs, signaling sell-off months after World Series appearance
description: The deal in part signals a Blue Jays selloff at the MLB trade deadline, months after they took the Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7 of the World Series.
fullText:
The Toronto Blue Jays have traded starting pitcher Kevin Gausman to the Chicago Cubs, signaling a sell-off at the MLB trade deadline months after they took the Dodgers to extra innings in Game 7 of the World Series.

The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal and Mitch Bannon reported the trade on Sunday, hours before Monday's 6 p.m. ET trade deadline. In return, according to the report, the Blue Jays will receive outfielder Brett Bateman and infielder Ty Southisene, both prospects.

The move in part cements a season of disappointment for the Blue Jays, who started 2026 with hopes of competing for the AL East title and returning to the postseason. Instead, they've entered the stretch run in last place in the division at 52-60 with long-shot hopes of competing for a wild-card spot.

Whether the Blue Jays would be sellers at the deadline or hold steady for a shot at the postseason was unclear before the All-Star break. But they lost five of their first six games coming out of the break, including three to the AL East-leading Tampa Bay Rays.

Gausman is playing on the final season of a five-year, $110 million contract. He was a prime candidate for a deadline deal to a contending team seeking a contributor with an expiring contract.

A two-time All-Star, Gausman isn't at his peak form at 35 years old. But he's been a reliable starter for much of his career, including this season as one of MLB's leaders in starts and innings pitched.

Gausman provides the Cubs with a mid-rotation option days after they designated veteran Jameson Taillon for assignment.

Taillon, 34, was in the midst of a career-worst season with a 5.92 ERA and 25 home runs allowed. Chicago traded Taillon to Toronto in a separate deal earlier Sunday for cash considerations or a player to be named later.

Taillon pitched 76 innings for the Cubs this season, and his departure left Chicago with a hole in their rotation. Gausman, who's made 14 postseason appearances, slots in for what the Cubs hope is an upgrade for the stretch run and a likely playoff appearance.

The Cubs leave a 2-1 loss to the Yankees on Sunday at 63-49, in control of first place in the NL wild-card standings with a four-game cushion over second. They're 6.5 game behind the Brewers for first place in the NL Central.

Per MLB Pipeline, Southisene ranked as Chicago's No. 13 prospect, and Bateman rated at No. 21. Neither are in MLB Pipeline's top 100 overall prospects. They're both now building blocks for Toronto's future.

The Chicago Cubs spent the days leading up to the MLB trade deadline searching for a starting pitcher capable of making a difference in October.

Chicago is acquiring veteran right-hander Kevin Gausman in a trade with the Toronto Blue Jays, ESPN’s Jeff Passan reported Sunday. Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic and Mitch Bannon were first to report the agreement.

The players heading back to Toronto were not immediately revealed.

The move gives the Cubs an experienced arm for the stretch run after the organization made upgrading its rotation a deadline priority. Although Gausman has not produced his best numbers this season, his track record and ability to miss bats make him a potentially significant addition.

Gausman owns a 5-10 record with a 4.38 ERA across 23 starts this season. He has recorded 127 strikeouts and 36 walks over 127.1 innings while posting a 1.29 WHIP.

The Chicago Cubs are acquiring right-hander Kevin Gausman in a trade with the Toronto Blue Jays, a source tells to ESPN. The Cubs have sought a playoff-caliber starting pitcher all deadline, and now they've landed one. First on the news was @Ken_Rosenthal and @MitchBannon.

— Jeff Passan (@JeffPassan) August 3, 2026

Those numbers may not immediately jump off the page, but Gausman has shown encouraging signs recently. The 35-year-old allowed only one earned run over 5.2 innings against the St. Louis Cardinals on Saturday. He surrendered nine hits but avoided major damage, issuing one walk and striking out four in Toronto’s 5-1 victory.

Gausman also worked six innings against the Boston Red Sox in his previous start, allowing three earned runs while striking out six. Across his final two appearances for the Blue Jays, he recorded a 3.09 ERA with 10 strikeouts and only two walks in 11.2 innings. He joins Chicago with 385 major league appearances, including 345 starts. The two-time All-Star has compiled 2,081 strikeouts across more than 2,000 career innings while pitching for the Baltimore Orioles, Atlanta Braves, Cincinnati Reds, San Francisco Giants and Blue Jays.

Gausman also has experience on the postseason stage. He has appeared in 10 playoff games during his career, including eight starts.

MORE: Dodgers close to acquiring Tarik Skubal in blockbuster three-player trade

The Cubs entered Sunday with a 61-51 record after a 2-1 loss to the New York Yankees. They remain firmly in the National League playoff race but needed another reliable starter to strengthen their chances of making a deep run.

Gausman gives Chicago a veteran who can absorb innings, generate strikeouts and potentially start an important postseason game.

He also arrives with another year remaining on the five-year, $110 million contract he signed with Toronto before the 2022 season. Gausman is scheduled to earn $23 million in 2027, meaning this is more than a short-term rental for the Cubs.

For the Blue Jays, the trade signals a different direction. Toronto fell to 52-60 with Saturday’s loss to St. Louis and entered Sunday 13.5 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East.

Rather than holding onto Gausman for another season, the Blue Jays elected to move one of their most accomplished starters and add to their future.

The full return will ultimately help determine how the trade is evaluated. For now, however, the immediate message is clear: The Cubs believe they can contend this season, and they have added one of the most established pitchers available to help them do it.

fullText:
The Atlanta Braves have struck again in the trade market and this time, they are bringing a starting pitcher to town. According to MLB Insider Robert Murray of FanSided, the Braves are picking up RHP Tyler Mahle from the Giants in exchange for RHP Anthony Molina.

So far this season, Mahle has put up a 5.13 ERA (125 ERA-) with a 4.38 FIP (108 FIP-) over 18 starts and 94.2 innings pitched so far with the Giants. He signed there as a free agent for one year and $10 million after spending a couple of seasons with Texas and he earned that contract after making 16 starts for the Rangers in 2025 (86.2 innings pitched) and producing a 2.18 ERA (54 ERA-) with a 3.37 FIP (80 FIP-).

Either way, he’s a starting pitcher who’s been able to at least reach the fifth inning in 16 of his 18 starts — though he did have a wobble in his last outing on this past Saturday, which is when he gave up five runs in 5.2 innings against the Padres. title: Take a look at Florida alumnus Christian Scott's 2026 MLB season stats
description: Take a look at how former Florida Gators and current New York Mets has performed in his second season of major league action.
fullText:
Former Florida baseball standout Christian Scott has had a strong showing during his 2026 campaign with the New York Mets so far.

Originally drafted by the Mets in the 5th round of the 2021 MLB Draft with the 142nd overall pick, the right-handed pitcher's ascent into big league ball hit a major roadblock in 2024, when he underwent a hybridized surgery that combined a traditional Tommy John ligament replacement with a stabilizing internal brace that caused him to miss all of the 2025 campaign.

Prior to his injury, Scott threw 47 1/3 innings for New York, posting an 0-3 record with a 4.56 ERA, 4.60 FIP and 1.20 WHIP while striking out 39 against 12 walks issued across that stretch for 0.4 fWAR. He had been a breakout prospect for the franchise up to that point, rising from unranked on the team's 2023 top 30 prospects list to No. 5 heading into 2024.

So far in 2026, Scott has not only picked up where he left off, he has also made some significant strides in several categories, putting up a 3-3 record with a tidy 2.99 ERA along with a solid 3.47 FIP and 1.24 WHIP over 69 1/3 innings of work for an fWAR of 1.5. While his walks per nine have regressed from 2.3 to 3.9, the Coconut Creek, Florida, native's home runs per nine have improved from 1.5 to 0.9 and strikeouts per nine have lept from 7.4 to 11.0.

According to Statcast, Scott's overall pitching run value ranks in the 63rd percentile among major league pitchers, with his fastball run value checking in the 76th percentile. His breaking ball and offspeed run values rate below average, coming in at 48th and 36th, respectively.

Scott's primary weapon is his four-seam fastball, which he employs half the time and sits just a hair above the MLB average at 95.4 mph; he also offers a cut fastball (17%) and barely used sinker (2%). His two breaking balls are a sweeper (22%) and curveball (6%), while the splitter (4%) represents his only offspeed offering.

The former Gator excels in several of Statcast's categories, checking into the 89th percentile in strikeout rate as well as his extension. Other areas where he rates higher than the average hurler are hard-hit percentage (77th), average exit velocity (74th), expected batting average (73rd) and barrel percentage (72nd), while his chase percentage (27th), walk percentage (25th) and groundball percentage (11th) land on the lower end of the scale.

The 27-year-old righty dealt with an injury this summer that shelved him on the injured list for a stint — a hip impingement that caused him to miss some time from mid to late June. Since then, he has maintained his spot in the rotation, putting up a 2.83 ERA, 2.96 FIP and 1.08 WHIP with 38 strikeouts and 11 walks over 28 2/3 innings.

Despite Scott's success this season, the Mets have floundered to a 47-65 record, landing them in the basement of the National League West division despite having the second-largest payroll in all of baseball.

Over 116 2/3 innings stretching across 24 appearances — all starts — Scott has posted a 3.63 ERA, 3.93 FIP and 1.23 WHIP for New York, amassing a 3-6 record along the way. So far, he has averaged 9.57 strikeouts against 3.24 walks per nine innings, along with 1.16 home runs per nine, and has accumulated a total of 2.0 fWAR.

title: Assessing the Dodgers trade deadline priorities
description: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across MLB. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Dodgers fans and fans across the country. fullText:
Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across MLB. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Dodgers fans and fans across the country. 

What do you get the team with the most talent in the sport? We asked you guys, and a new catcher was at the top of the wishlist, taking 47 percent of the votes. Before getting into what that might entail, let’s take a moment to appreciate the absurdity that not a single vote was cast for a position player (outside of catcher) — rightfully so, with no open spot on this roster the team could realistically hope to improve on That and other priorities, of course, while trying to improve its World Series odds.

The remaining 53 percent who didn’t vote for catcher were nearly split between starting and relief pitching. Both units share the exciting prospect of reinforcements on the way or recently arrived, with Edwin Díaz just activated and Blake Snell not far behind him. While any bullpen could always use an extra arm, the starting staff has this looming cloud over it with questions regarding the availability of Shohei Ohtani.

Assessing options on the market for these positions of “need,” with Will Smith’s rehab finally showing promising signs, the Dodgers may very well limit themselves to less splashy options. As we covered before here, Victor Caratini and Ryan Jeffers of the Twins may represent the best targets. A pending free agent, Jeffers wouldn’t cost a king’s ransom, unlike other more exciting controllable catchers, and the veteran Caratini would represent a safety net type of acquisition.

On the starting pitching front, with Eric Lauer thriving since being acquired by the Dodgers and Snell returning, it feels like a Tarik Skubal or bust kind of situation. Sure, there are other options who could prove to be an improvement over what the Dodgers have on the backend of the rotation right now, at least in terms of ceiling, but they’re not particularly likely moves. Unfortunately for the Dodgers, some of the better potentially available relievers at the deadline play for the Padres, making for a difficult deal as San Diego would inevitably prefer to move them to someone else. Everyone might want to talk about Mason Miller as the dream target, but pending free agent Adrian Morejón might be a more feasible acquisition and a great one in his own right.

Whether the target is a starter or a reliever, perhaps the best team to talk with is the Mets. While their record is atrocious, the Mets don’t lack in high-end reliever quality, with Brooks Raley and Luke Weaver pitching great and firmly available. A.J. Minter was also in this group, but he was the first to go, traded to the Twins on Thursday night. In the unlikely scenario the Dodgers want to add a starter not named Skubal, Clay Holmes ticks a lot of boxes, having recently returned from an injury and heading for the open market at the end of the year.
