title: MLB trade deadline: Latest rumors on Tarik Skubal, Hunter Greene, and more
description: What are the latest rumors ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline?
fullText:
If you believe Jeff Passan, today is the day we will start seeing trades ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline, which arrives Monday.

So let’s spin around the rumors again.

Wednesday afternoon, Tarik Skubal exited the Detroit Tigers’ game against the Baltimore Orioles in the top of the seventh, having given up a two-run single. He left to a standing ovation from the Detroit faithful, who were wondering like the rest of us whether it was his last outing for the Tigers. He exited having handed the Detroit bullpen a 7-1 lead with two outs and a pair of runners aboard.

What happened after that is, according to one MLB executive, the final “sign” that the Tigers need to move their ace at the deadline.

Baltimore scored four more runs in the inning, and went on to win 10-9 in extras. Despite recording his 1,000th strikeout in the performance, Skubal received a no-decision for his efforts.

“If there was ever a sign that the Tigers should trade Skubal, that was it. The offers should start flowing in any minute,” said one NL executive to MLB insider Mark Feinsand.

Feinsand was not the only one reporting that a deal would be happening. ESPN’s Jeff Passan declared Skubal “will be traded” in his MLB Trade Deadline preview as well.

So what teams could be making a move for the ace? As we outlined yesterday the Milwaukee Brewers are among the suitors, and Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that the Chicago Cubs are expected to make a run at the left-hander. But according to Passan, when it comes to potential suitors they are “all almost resigned to the idea that the Los Angeles Dodgers are going to get Tarik Skubal.”

A potential reason for that? The lingering health issues for Shohei Ohtani. With the superstar dealing with left knee and right bicep issues, it has put his time on the bump on hold. His last start came on July 3, and manager Dave Roberts indicated earlier this week that his throwing program is on hold. “Trying to mitigate that, we stopped the throwing, stopped the bullpens — hopefully, No. 1, take care of the knee and then not have him try to create velocity with the arm that’s not 100%,” Roberts said.

With Ohtani on the shelf — as a pitcher — that could mean a big push for Skubal from the Dodgers.

If you’re looking for a sleeper team in the Skubal sweepstakes, keep an eye on Tampa Bay. The Rays saw left-hander Shane McClanahan leave his start on Thursday with “back tightness,” and while it is not considered a “long-term” issue, there is an opening for Tampa Bay. As one MLB source told MLB.com, “[t]he Brewers, Rays and Dodgers have the most high-end prospects to move. It would be somewhat surprising if he didn’t wind up with one of those three teams.”

While Skubal will command the headlines, another top arm could be on the move.

According to MLB.com, there is a “50-50” chance that the Cincinnati Reds move flame-thrower Hunter Greene ahead of the MLB Trade Deadline. Greene missed the first half of the season following surgery to remove bone chips from his right elbow, as he put off the surgery last season and threw through the discomfort, option for an injection rather than surgery.

He ultimately went under the knife in the spring, costing him the start to 2026. Since returning he has gone 2-2 with a 7.06 ERA in four starts this season.

But this is a former All-Star, who is under club control for the next few seasons. He signed a six-year extension with Cincinnati in 2023, and is controlled through 2028. Greene is owed $15 million in 2027, $16 million in 2028, and has a $21 million club option for 2029, and his contract comes with a $2 million buyout.

His health is probably the biggest concern, as he has missed time beyond the recent surgery. Tommy John surgery in 2018 cost him the entire 2019 Minor League campaign, and he has lost time due to shoulder and lower-body issues.

“Health,” said one MLB executive to MLB.com about the concern. “He falls into the high quality and moderate-to-low quantity category.”

Still, during his 2024 All-Star campaign, he went 9-5 with a 2.75 ERA, earning Cy Young votes. Teams that miss on Skubal could be enticed to bet on that talent — at that low cost — for the next few years.

Our friends at Battery Power are taking about Greene as well:

As we noted yesterday, the New York Yankees are one of several teams looking for help behind the plate at the MLB Trade Deadline.

According to longtime MLB insider Jon Heyman, the Yankees have inquired with the Baltimore Orioles about Adley Rutschman, but from the outside looking in it would seem unlikely that Mike Elias would move the catcher within the division:

Yankees are among many teams to check on 3-time All-Star/switch-hitting catcher Adley Rutschman. NYY is casting a wide net for catching need. Ryan Jeffers, pending free agent, seemed logical but Twins suggest they’re a buyer now. Tyler Stephenson, others are on NYY list

— Jon Heyman (@JonHeyman) July 29, 2026

However, Passan reported on his podcast earlier this week that the Orioles are at least “open” to moving players such as Rutschman. Open is one thing, but making a deal … and one to the Yankees … is another.

Colorado Rockies catcher Hunter Goodman is another option generating buzz, given last year’s slash line of .278/.323/.520, but the fact that he has three arbitration years coming up before he becomes a free agent in 2030 has pushed the asking price up.

With the Los Angeles Dodgers running away with things in the NL West, the San Diego Padres sit in third place, 14 games back in the division.

But at one game over .500, the Padres are just two games out in the NL Wild Card chase, so moving a key player ahead of hte deadline does not seem likely.

Until you remember general manager A.J. Preller is involved

After swinging last year’s biggest move, the deal with the Athletics for closer Mason Miller, could Preller really turn around and trade him at the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline? According to Passan it is at least possible, but Preller has been telling teams that no prospect can be listed as off limits in such a deal.

With the New York Mets mired at the bottom of the NL standings, they are expected to move some players ahead of the deadline.

One of them could be right-hander Clay Holmes.

Holmes has not pitched in the majors since mid-May, when he suffered a broken right fibula, but was 4-4 in his nine starts with a 2.39 ERA and WHIP of 1.101. He pitched four scoreless innings for Low-A St. Lucia earlier this week, a game that was attended by scouts from several teams including the Yankees, White Sox, Phillies, Rays, Rangers, Dodgers, according to The Athletic.

He is set to hit free agency at the end of the season, but is still expected to have a “strong” market. One AL executive told FanSided that “[i]t would be a surprise if he didn’t [get traded].”

title: 2026 MLB Trade Deadline Near With Most Teams Rocking Same Parity Boat
description: The next five days will decide the future of many MLB players and teams. The trade deadline is August 3. Who knows who goes where and who doesn't by 6 p.m. ET on Monday?
fullText:
The next five days will determine the future fate of many MLB players and teams. The 2026 MLB Trade Deadline is August 3, and who goes where or stays put by 6 p.m. ET on Monday is tied to which teams win or lose until then.

There isn’t a team in any sport on any level on the planet that isn’t wishing to improve. In that sense, all 30 MLB teams would like to be “buyers” adding better and more expensive players by Monday. Some simply do not have the talent needed to exchange or the money to pay in return, however. Those clubs would usually be classified as “sellers” seeking to cut payroll and add promising prospects in hopes of rebuilding for the future.

Except that in 2026, the future could be now – given the results of the next five days. The best possible prizes, pitchers Tarik Skubal and Mason Miller and shortstop C.J. Abrams could be retained to help their teams keep winning or dealt to wave the white flag for 2026 with hopes of waving a pennant in 2027.

Each league has 12 teams reasonably in the running for one of six playoff spots apiece. Therefore, only six teams total are basically out of it and presumably more eager to be “sellers” of their best players.

Yet if those “best players” were performing real well in 2026, those clubs would not be in the predicament of essentially saying sayonara, see you next year. There’s not a high demand for the cream of the tail-end crop.

It’s a classic catch-22 scenario – which brings to mind a humorous anecdote. When asked why defensively-challenged Dick Stuart was nicknamed “Catch 22” in the 1960s, a teammate replied, “Because if you made 50 throws to him, he’d catch 22.”

The odds should be higher that the majority of MLB teams will make a player move or two by the impending deadline. Except this year, determining who goes where is tougher than usual since clubs are traditionally unwilling to deal with a team it is battling in the standings. So in 2026, perhaps we should look for more trades involving AL and NL teams.

Conversely, the “I’ll help you, since you are not in direct competition” thinking may restrict the number of trades as it curtails the number of possibilities.

It sounds undecisive, unpredictable and a bit screwy only because it is.

In 2026, the Angels, Athletics, Blue Jays, Cardinals, Giants, Mets, Rockies and Royals appear to be most likely sellers. A couple other teams could join that group this weekend.

Veteran infielder Luis Arraez is often mentioned as likely to be dealt by San Francisco despite his .326 batting average, second in the National League. The Giants (45-61) are 9.5 games out of a possible wild-card spot and Arraez is due to become an unrestricted free agent in 2027.

A contender needing offense could want the three-time batting champion who since the end of 2022 has played for Minnesota, Miami, San Diego and San Francisco. Miami’s 2024 trade of Arraez got prospects that have helped the Marlins improve.

Those needing a pitcher and willing to pay off a contract could contact Toronto about Kevin Gausman. The 35-year-old will be owed $7 million this year after the deadline. Since May 23, he is 0-7 to put his record at 4-10 as the defending AL champion Blue Jays are five games behind Cleveland for the final wild-card spot.

In his loss streak, Gausman got only 14 runs (2.0 a game) of support. So a rival GM could figure, “He is pitching well enough to win with us.”

Then again, if Toronto runs the table the next five days, the Blue Jays may be back in true contention and decide to add players. It’s that close and questionable.

Teams on the cusp of contending today could be out of it or on a winning streak by Monday. Sitting on the fence right now, contemplating various scenarios are the Marlins, Nationals, Orioles, Padres, Tigers and Twins.

That leaves 16 buyers, though a bad five days by some of them could completely change their plans.

A great stretch already altered the Boston Red Sox’ fortunes and thinking. A 15-game winning streak and 20-2 record from June 25 to July 22 took them from last place into solid playoff contention. So the Red Sox fired an “early” trade shot.

Boston made the first buyers’ salvo on July 26 by acquiring infielder Curtis Mead from Washington for pitcher Connelly Early. "This move makes our major league roster better," Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Breslow told reporters. “We think this is a move to make us better in 2026 and we’ll continue to look for these opportunities.”

Alas, Mead is out with a broken left wrist, incurred when hit by a pitch in his second time at bat for Boston.

Six clubs already have 60 or more wins with less than 60 games to play. The Los Angeles Dodgers (67 wins), Milwaukee Brewers (66), Tampa Bay Rays (62), Atlanta Braves (62), New York Yankees (60) and Chicago Cubs (60) are likely to enter a different competition in the coming days – trying to beat out each other in acquiring needed players.

The Rays are ruling the rugged AL East, helped by deadline deals of a year ago. Those that buy best now could leave others in their wake and wave bye-bye.

The Seattle Mariners did it last year by acquiring Josh Naylor and Eugenio Suarez from Arizona near the deadline. The duo combined for 22 homers, 64 RBI and 22 stolen bases (19 in 19 tries by the hefty Naylor) as Seattle went from five games back to winning the AL West.

Traditionally, the Dodgers and Yankees have both the minor-league prospect supply and revenue needed to get whoever they want. The Braves and Cubs usually are pro-active, too, while the Brewers and Rays often seek more prospects in favor of paring payroll and increasing future forecasts.

Milwaukee and Tampa Bay may jump into the foray this time. Both have minor-league systems loaded with prospects each accumulated at deadlines in recent years and could flip this time. Tampa Bay also has a new ownership group that gives the franchise the ability to put money where its’ wish list is for the first time.

It is all too topsy-turvy to predict who is going to do what within the next five days – both on the playing field and on the telephone wheeling and dealing.

Hall of Fame pitcher Satchel Paige once said, “Ain’t no man can avoid being born average, but there ain’t no man that got to be common.” He meant that men are born in parity, but can work to rise above it.

The 2026 MLB Trade Deadline gives teams – and by extension their fans – the opportunity to boldly break from current parity, go for it all, and perhaps experience the thrill of being a champion.

title: Cody Bellinger injury adds urgency to Yankees trade deadline plans
description: Cody Bellinger's Grade 2 hamstring strain adds pressure on the Yankees to upgrade before the MLB trade deadline.
fullText:
Cody Bellinger’s worse-than-expected hamstring strain adds a new layer to the Yankees’ trade deadline period.

Diagnosed on Monday with a Grade 2 left hamstring strain, Bellinger’s four-to-six week timeline to return puts him back in the Yankees’ lineup sometime in September.

But even with Bellinger, a compromised Yankees lineup – no Aaron Judge since June 2, no Giancarlo Stanton since April 25 – had become a deeper issue.

Before their 9-5 win against the White Sox on Monday night, the second-place Yankees were 14-19 since June 19, averaging 3.27 runs per game.

Prior to that, the Yankees were averaging 5.27 runs per game and leading the AL East by 3.5 games.

Of course, every pinstriped hope of a deep October run is connected to Judge’s return.

And we’re still waiting on the second re-imaging of Judge’s fractured first right rib, and for his clearance just to begin baseball activity.

With Stanton, the constant he’s-getting-closer narrative should never limit the pursuit of more offense.

Still, impact bats are tough to find in this trade market, and you wonder about the appeal for the Yanks to absorb a bad contract or another DH-only type.

In recent days, potential offensive targets in Cincinnati’s Spencer Steer (wrist), San Francisco’s Casey Schmitt (knee) and even A’s catcher Shea Langeliers (knee), a longshot trade candidate, have receded due to injury.

A right-handed hitting outfielder is a better Yankee fit, and Kansas City has two impending free agents in Starling Marte and Lane Thomas. And the Mets' Tyrone Taylor is an increasingly intriguing option.

Elsewhere, if the Tigers choose to trade lefty ace Tarik Skubal, might they also be inclined to deal fellow impending free agent Gleyber Torres?

But the defensive fit in the Bronx is an issue, which also applies to Padres’ lefty-hitting second baseman Luis Arraez, also in his free agent walk year.

Still, the Bellinger situation doesn’t alter the Yanks’ top areas to upgrade.

The search for a swing-and-miss reliever and a right-handed hitting catcher could take the Yankees right up to Monday’s MLB trade deadline.

With an .856 OPS in nine games since his return from a left hamate bone fracture, right-handed hitting Minnesota catcher Ryan Jeffers – an impending free agent – is one possible target.

But the Twins are also three games back in the middling AL Central and one game behind for the last AL wild card spot entering Tuesday, so Jeffers’ trade status remains an interesting case.

And if there’s one huge trade to be made this deadline period, San Diego closer Mason Miller is the all-in candidate, with monumental end-game impact and team control through 2029.

If the Padres are inclined, lefty reliever Adrian Morejon – a free agent after this season – is a solid trade candidate. Plus, the Yanks’ past solid relationships with Luke Weaver and the rehabbing Clay Holmes (leg fracture) puts the Mets in play as a potential trade partner.

Bellinger’s absence further weakens the Yankees defensively, an overall area that needs to be addressed.

With appreciation of his utility value, Max Schuemann is an infielder playing out of position in left field, where Bellinger’s 19 defensive runs saved this year has boosted one of the league’s best pitching staffs.

For all his hard work and leadership, Amed Rosario is a liability at any defensive position, and he’s been less of a lefty masher this year, batting .197 overall in his last 25 games.

Top Yankees’ prospect George Lombard Jr. has initially struggled to hit each time he’s moved up a level, and you’d be asking a lot for him to debut in a pennant race.

But his plus-defensive skills at shortstop make him a prime candidate for an August call-up, as one more way to bolster the club’s pitching – its primary strength.

At last year’s deadline, the Yankees became a much better team down the stretch, in part, because of third baseman Ryan McMahon’s defensive presence.

Lombard could have that kind of impact even if he bats .208, which was McMahon’s average in 54 games after his arrival last summer from Colorado.

title: Why the Tigers should (and shouldn't) trade star ace Tarik Skubal at the 2026 MLB trade deadline
description: The Tigers have a decision to make on Tarik Skubal. Here's what they will have to consider.
fullText:
Why the Tigers should (and shouldn't) trade star ace Tarik Skubal at the 2026 MLB trade deadline originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Every contender is looking for an upgrade ahead of the MLB trade deadline, but no player might be more coveted than Tigers ace Tarik Skubal.

The two-time Cy Young Award winner is a pending free agent and has been viewed as a trade candidate since the Tigers fell as many as 16 games under .500 early in the season.

With better results in recent weeks, however, Detroit could still hold on to Skubal and try to make another run at the postseason.

What's the right decision? Here are the cases for and against the Tigers trading Skubal.

MORE:16 players who could be traded by MLB deadline

Barring a drastic change of heart, the Tigers aren't going to re-sign Skubal. The two sides have reportedly remained far apart in contract talks, and the record-setting $13 million gap between Skubal and the Tigers during the arbitration process was likely the final nail in the coffin.

With that in mind, if the Tigers held on to Skubal for the remainder of the season, what would it take to make that decision a success? If it's strictly a World Series win, you can probably take that idea off the table. Not only are the Tigers still comfortably under .500, but there isn't any reason to believe they have the talent to win a championship.

Is it a trip to the World Series? The American League is wide open, but if the Tigers couldn't get past the ALDS last season, that's hard to envision. If the ALCS, which is also unlikely, would justify keeping Skubal, Detroit should think long and hard about whether that's a worthwhile goal.

From a practical standpoint, making the postseason is unlikely. The Tigers are facing a six-game deficit in the AL Central, which is manageable, but they have three teams ahead of them rather than just one team to chase down. Detroit is closer in the wild-card race but faces the same dynamic, with four teams separating the franchise from the final wild-card team.

Skubal is coming off two excellent starts, his best since returning from the injured list. If he isn't coming back next season, it makes more sense to go get some value instead of holding on to a pipe dream of a magical October run.

MORE:Tarik Skubal makes trade deadline stance clear

The Tigers might not want their reputation to be that of a team that had a chance at the postseason and threw it away by dealing a beloved ace. With the American League so mediocre and the final wild-card team hovering near .500, Detroit could set a goal of 83-85 wins and enter a wild-card series with one of baseball's elite pitchers setting the tone in Game 1.

Looking around the AL, only two teams are more than six games over .500: the Rays, who still have to prove that they can win in October, and the Yankees, who have held their own in the second half but are struggling to find any offense with Aaron Judge, Giancarlo Stanton and now Cody Bellinger injured.

The Tigers may see 2026 as their year to make a run in October — if they can get there. Getting there with Skubal is challenging. Getting there without Skubal is just about impossible.

The value Detroit would have been able to get for Skubal earlier in his contract would have been immense, but the value for him as a rental might not be enough to totally transform the organization. If that's the case, the Tigers can show their fans that they aren't willing to quit on the season and give this group a real chance to make a push.

MORE: Every Cy Young winner in the history of the award

Skubal is set to be a free agent after this season. The Tigers ace is making $32 million after the salary arbitration process ruled in his favor over Detroit's significantly lower $19 million offer.

That gap has convinced most fans that Skubal is headed elsewhere in free agency in the winter, and Skubal recently made comments that alluded to some lingering tension between himself and the front office.

If the Tigers decide their best bet is to keep Skubal and try to engineer a miraculous postseason run, they run the risk of getting no talent back for one of the best pitchers in baseball, much like the Angels when they held onto Shohei Ohtani at the 2023 deadline.

title: Why do minor leaguers keep chasing the MLB? Ask Smokies infielder Ed Howard
description: Former Cubs first-round pick Ed Howard's career hasn't unfolded the way he wishes it did. Why Howard continues to chase his MLB dream against the odds
fullText:
Ed Howard knows what people see when they look at his career: a hometown kid from the South Side of Chicago, selected 16th overall by the Cubs, and once destined for an infield spot at Wrigley Field.

They also see the injuries that followed.

What many don't see is why the Knoxville Smokies infielder keeps playing the sport he dedicated his life to at 5 years old, even as the odds grew longer.

"I probably could have walked away from the game, and nobody probably would have got mad at me," Howard told Knox News. "But that never occurred. I never even thought of that because I wanted to reach my dream."

Somewhere along the way − in a career defined by surgeries, setbacks and nearly four years of rebuilding − Howard stopped worrying about whether baseball had treated him fairly and instead focused on where it could still take him.

Acceptance is something he never expected to learn. And after a two-month stint in a hospital bed, he came to understand a lesson many athletes learn much earlier: Talent alone is not enough to shield a career from adversity.

"I just always wanted to write my own story," he said. "I don't want the injury to define it."

The South Bend Cubs had erased a five-run deficit against the Fort Wayne TinCaps on May 10, 2022, when Howard hit a grounder to shortstop. With one out in the ninth inning, he collided with the first baseman, fell to the ground and tried to stand back up. He couldn't move.

Trainers helped him to the clubhouse, where his mother and grandmother found him distraught in a ripped jersey.

"I was just angry, upset," Howard said. "Who was I upset at? I was just upset at the world. I didn't know."

Howard tore the labrum in his left hip, dislocated the joint and fractured the posterior wall in his pelvis. Eight days later, a titanium plate was inserted with screws.

He spent two months glued to a hospital bed, receiving blood-thinner injections in his stomach and watching his left leg shrink from not being used. He had to re-learn how to walk.

The physical recovery was measurable. The mental recovery was not.

Howard spent the first 18 years of his life believing hard work could solve almost anything. Baseball wasn't part of his family, but he was always taught that "if you really want something, just put in the work."

That's what carried him through the 2014 Little League World Series and later helped him become one of the top prep players in the 2020 MLB Draft as a shortstop from Mount Carmel High School in Chicago.

But the injury wasn't something Howard could overcome with effort. When you're out of action as a baseball player, he said, that's "all that's running through your mind."

His mind was ready to rehab and never talk about the injury again. But recovery doesn't follow a definite timeline.

"I wanted to come out like a rocket and just be the same 18-year-old kid that I was," Howard said. "But it doesn't work like that."

When he returned ahead of schedule roughly 10 months later, he collected two doubles as part of a three-hit night. Though it seemed like Howard had returned from the outside, the underlying challenges persisted.

"I'm limping," he said. "I'm struggling in my apartment. I got to get up and use the restroom in the middle of the night and I can't get there."

Patience was the biggest lesson Howard took away from his injury. Prior to getting hurt, everything with baseball was always moving forward.

"At 18," Howard said, "you want everything when you want it."

Rather than dwelling on why the injury happened, Howard began asking what could still become of it. He hit his first home run at Covenant Health Park in Knoxville on July 9, proving to himself that he could still play the game at a high level.

Faith deepened during the years away from the field, Howard said, and his family became the foundation. The internal belief never left.

"Nobody knows you more than you know yourself," he said.

Howard stopped worrying about outside opinions. He believes in who he was. The work ethic, mindset and drive remained consistent, he said: "I'm still the same guy."

As the hometown kid with all the potential, the 24-year-old smiles when asked about pressure. He welcomes the feeling.

"Pressure is a privilege," Howard said.

Once a high-profile shortstop, Howard hopes to play in games where expectations are high again. Expectations mean people still believe in him.

"I pray that one day there are more pressure moments in my career," he said.

Howard still believes he can make it to Wrigley Field. Though injuries changed his body and altered his timeline, his performance is meant to satisfy an audience of one.

"At the end of the day," he said, "I'm really doing this to prove it to myself."

His present-day self looks back at the young Howard − angry at the world in the Four Winds Field locker room in South Bend, Indiana. On the winding road back from his 2022 injury, he has discovered everything happens when it's supposed to happen. He just had to accept it first.

"I just want to keep going," he said, "until I can look up and almost smile and laugh at him."

title: Tarik Skubal, Tigers win again. That's bad news for rest of MLB | Opinion
description: The Tigers just keep winning. Will Tarik Skubal, who was dominant Friday, still be in Detroit on the other side of the trade deadline?
fullText:
Tarik Skubal's next start at Comerica Park could be his last as a Detroit Tiger. Yet the way he's been pitching and the Tigers keep winning, the chances keep increasing that he'll stick around the Motor City a couple more months.

Skubal made quick work of the Kansas City Royals Friday, July 24, striking out a season-high 12 and mowing through 7⅓ innings on 91 pitches as the Tigers defeated the Royals 2-1 for their 12th win in 16 games.

The victory moved Detroit to 50-54, the closest they've been to the .500 mark since they were 19-23 on May 12. They remained within six games of first place in the American League Central, and four games of the final wild card berth.

And that could be bad news for the rest of Major League Baseball's contenders.

More: Five MLB teams who will be most aggressive at 2026 trade deadline

Skubal, 29 and a free agent after this season, is by far the most anticipated potential trade chip this year. After the Tigers sank 16 games below .500 on May 31 as Skubal worked his way back from elbow surgery, it was widely assumed Skubal, if healthy, would certainly be available by the Aug. 3 trade deadline.

Skubal is plenty healthy and starting to approach his two-time Cy Young Award-winning form. Trouble is, the Tigers are playing far better ball, too.

They are 28-16 since June 1, and with each win they put on the board, must ponder the impact dealing their ace would have on their fan base.

For now, Detroit is enjoying Skubal's greatness, as 40,638 turned out on a 77-degree night at Comerica Park to watch him work.

Skubal allowed just six baserunners, giving up four hits and two walks, and his 12 strikeouts were his most since punching out a dozen Athletics in an 8-3 loss on Aug. 25, 2025. In seven starts since returning from May elbow surgery, Skubal has a 2.70 ERA and a 65-6 strikeout-walk ratio.

And he's only picking up steam.

Skubal was coming off a seven-inning shutout effort against the Los Angeles Angels, and another dominant start like his last two, and it'd be hard to dispute he's returned to his Cy Young-winning form.

On one hand, that greatly enhances his trade value. On the other? Well, the Tigers compete in the notoriously weak AL Central, in one of the worst seasons the AL overall has experienced perhaps this century. Holding on to Skubal gives them a far better shot at a third consecutive playoff berth.

That's why each Tigers game from now until the deadline takes on added import. For now, Skubal is lined up to pitch Wednesday, July 29 against the Baltimore Orioles at Comerica Park.

After that, the Tigers hit the road and Skubal's next start will come shortly after the deadline. And every time he takes the ball, it seems to enhance the chances he'll be suiting up in a Tigers uniform Aug. 4.

Listed as 5-11, 170 pounds, Tronstein is undersized but regardless has big power and put up some of the best exit velocities at the MLB Draft Combine. He has an aggressive approach that Vanderbilt hitting coach Jason Esposito could help him tone down.

A high school shortstop, Tronstein is unlikely to surpass returning starter Ryker Waite. He could also fit at second base or the outfield, and the Commodores lost both starting corner outfielders in 2026. Whichever position he tries out, there will be lots of competition with fellow freshmen Gunner Skelton, Noah Wilson and Michael Holt, plus transfers Hunter Ray, Blaize Ward, Niko Brini and Bud Coombs.

Tronstein joining Vanderbilt's class means that the Commodores have six top-100 players in the class: Tronstein, Skelton, Wilson; pitchers Joseph Contreras and Bo Holloway and two-way player RJ Cope. That's the most since at least 2011, surpassing five top-100 freshmen in the 2018 class.

title: Cubs roster move: James Triantos called up, Kevin Alcántara optioned
description: The second-round pick of the Cubs in 2021 will make his MLB debut.
fullText:
This is a really interesting roster move.

James Triantos was the Cubs’ second-round pick in 2021 out of high school in Virginia. He had just turned 18, and went right to work in the Arizona Complex League, batting .327/.376/.594 in 25 games.

He rose through the system, hitting pretty well at every stop, but never really having a position. He played all three outfield positions as well as second base and third base. This year at Triple-A Iowa, Triantos is batting .306/.344/.440 (107-for-350) with 24 doubles, seven home runs and 18 stolen bases in 85 games.

The Cubs have called up Triantos, who is now 23, to join the 26-man active roster as the team opens a series in Pittsburgh. To make room on the 26-man active roster, outfielder/DH Kevin Alcántara was optioned to Iowa. This move has not yet been officially announced by the team, but Triantos posted on his Instagram story that he was being called up, and the Cubs transactions page shows that Alcántara was optioned on Thursday.

This move appears to acknowledge that Matt Shaw isn’t close to coming back, as Triantos plays basically the same positions Shaw does. This year Triantos has played mostly second base and third base and less outfield, while last year he played a fair amount of center field.

He’ll likely be a right-handed bat off the bench, occasional DH and fill in at various positions.

title: Yordan Alvarez competing for MLB Triple Crown after hitting 34th home run in Astros' 5-2 win over Marlins
description: Alvarez leads MLB in two of three Triple Crown categories, and all three in the AL.
fullText:
With 58 games remaining in the Houston Astros' 2026 season and two months left on the schedule, it might be too early to talk about Yordan Alvarez potentially winning a Triple Crown.

Yet after Alvarez hit his 34th home run of the season, it's not unreasonable to raise the possibility either. The Astros slugger batted 2-for-4 with 2 RBI in Houston's 5-2 win over the Miami Marlins.

Alvarez now leads MLB in homers, overtaking the Philadelphia Phillies' Kyle Schwarber. And he has four more than Ben Rice of the New York Yankees for the top spot in the AL.

With 77 RBI, Alvarez is one ahead of the Washington Nationals' CJ Abrams and Jordan Walker of the St. Louis Cardinals. And though he trails the Marlins' Otto Lopez (.332) for the MLB lead in batting average, his .328 mark leads the Tampa Bay Rays' Yandy Diaz (.308) by 20 points.

MLB's last Triple Crown winner was the Detroit Tigers' Miguel Cabrera, who led the AL with a .330 batting average, 44 homers and 139 RBI. But as might be expected, Alvarez doesn't want to talk about the Triple Crown right now.

"I'm just focused right now on playing ball," Alvarez said to MLB.com's Brian McTaggart. "There's more than two months remaining in the season, so I'm not going to talk anymore about the Triple Crown. I don't want to answer any more questions about the Triple Crown."

With the Astros fighting for a playoff spot, Alvarez is understandably reluctant to discuss individual achievements. Not to mention that talking about a thing makes it a thing that could present an obstacle to peak performance. Wednesday's win improved Houston's record to 50-54, two games behind the first-place Texas Rangers (51-51) in the AL West and 1.5 back from the Seattle Mariners (51-52) for second place. The Astros face more of an uphill climb in the AL wild-card race, 3.5 games from the league's third spot with four teams ahead of them — including the Boston Red Sox, who just finished a 15-game winning streak.

The Astros have won three consecutive games after sweeping the Marlins. However, they lost seven of 10 before that, including two of three to the Rangers, the team Houston is trying to catch in the AL West.

That skid raised questions about the Astros being sellers at the trade deadline, perhaps dealing off players like shortstop Jeremy Peña, third baseman Isaac Paredes or reliever Josh Hader. Yet Houston could just as easily be buyers at the deadline, looking to add pieces, including a starting pitcher, high-leverage reliever or outfield bat to provide a boost to its playoff chances.

"You get swept, you sweep somebody back, right?" said Astros manager Joe Espada, via MLB.com.

"That's a good bounceback win. That was good stuff," he added. "We bounced back very well against a good Marlins team. Beat one of the best pitchers in the game. I think our players, our team reacted very well after the way we played against Baltimore."

The Astros face another test this weekend with a three-game set at the Chicago White Sox (54-47).

fullText:
The New York Yankees are reportedly “set to sign Sebastian Perez for a $1.7 million signing bonus in the 2027 international drafting class,” states MLB International Reporter Wilber Sanchez, but Francys Romero was the first to report this news back in February. It was also mentioned by Sanchez in February that Perez originally had a deal in place with the Pittsburgh Pirates, but that the deal fell through, also adding that some scouts believe “he’s one of the best catchers in his draft class” and has lots of power and speed that could translate well to the big leagues one day, reported Sanchez.

MLB International Reporter Francys Romero was the first to report that the Yankees were the “expected team to sign Perez” to this deal, with Perez being a catcher out of Venezuela. Romero further added that at this time, back in February, the signing period doesn’t open until January 15th, 2027, and that this is considered to be “the first major agreement since the Yankees found a new international director of scouting”, stated Romero. Romero also added how Perez’s “original deal with the Pirates was for $1.3 million, but Perez’s representatives went back out on the market for a larger bonus deal”, reported Romero.

Romero has also described Perez’s scouting report as similar to Sanchez’s report today, noting that he hits for a lot of power (high exit velocity) and is an “excellent” defender behind the plate. Reporter Wilber Sanchez recently interviewed Perez to gather his thoughts. When discussing what it means to join the Yankees organization, Perez stated, “I feel good, I’m so excited to belong to the Yankees.” Perez even went on to add how he loved this organization growing up, and his goal is to make the Major Leagues within the next couple of years, Perez said.

The Yankees have changed their approach to international scouting and signing in recent months. The Yankees organization had “parted ways” with former director of scouting Danny Rowland, who had been the Yankees’ head director of international scouting for 15 seasons. Rowland signed international players such as Jasson Dominguez, Miguel Andujar, Luis Severino, and Roderick Arias, but there wasn’t a good track record of success in this department.

The Yankees felt it was best to go in a different direction, leading them to promote Mario Garza as the new director of international scouting this past offseason, a move that was officially announced on June 28th via a report from Yankees beat writer Bryan Hoch of MLB.com. Garza has been with the Yankees for up to 16 years and has reportedly worked in a variety of player development and coaching positions with the Yankees in their farm system, reported Hoch. The Yankees have taken a liking to Garza and his strategy as it relates to evaluating talent, as Hoch also reported Yankees General Manager Brian Cashman, when speaking about Garza, stated: “He knows our systems. He already knows all the personnel we want”, Cashman told Hoch.

The Yankees International Scouting Department has gotten to work recently. Not just with this reported deal expected in January, but also with the recent signing of Taiwanese pitcher Chien Fan Lai, who is fresh out of high school, has already reported to the Yankees Dominican Summer League Academy, and is currently in a throwing program. The Yankees’ overhaul in their international scouting department is a change they hope pays dividends 10-15 years down the line as new talent enters the Bronx in the foreseeable future.

fullText:
It has been 10 years since the loss of the Bakersfield Blaze, the last minor-league baseball team to play in Sam Lynn Ballpark with a Major League Baseball affiliation.

The Blaze was in Bakersfield from 1995 to 2016 and had affiliation with the Giants, Rays, Rangers, Reds and lastly, the Mariners. While the franchise is no longer around, there are present-day baseball connections — MLB connections — to note.

Tim Wheeler is a local sports statistician who works at numerous Bakersfield College and Cal State Bakersfield sporting events and had been working baseball games at Sam Lynn Ballpark, including the Blaze's entire run (1,500-plus games) before retiring from the current tenant, the independent Train Robbers, in 2025. He sent in an interesting list he recently researched.

He tracked down all former Bakersfield Blaze players who are currently playing professionally, either in MLB or in the minors and have MLB experience.

One player, New York Yankees pitcher Ryan Yarbrough, just faced the Los Angeles Dodgers on Sunday. L.A. was in New York for the first series after last week’s MLB All-Star Game.

Yarbrough, who pitched for the Blaze in 2015, is one of six current MLB players with Blaze ties and one of five pitchers. The others are the Colorado Rockies’ Michael Lorenzen (Blaze, 2013), San Diego Padres’ Wandy Peralta (2014), Washington Nationals’ Zack Littrell (2016) and current injured Dodgers relief pitcher Edwin Diaz (2015). The lone non-pitcher is Baltimore Orioles outfielder Tyler O’Neill (2015).

Wheeler also found three more Blaze players — all pitchers — who are currently in the minors, have MLB experience, but are not currently on the parent club’s 40-man roster. They are Ben Lively, Columbus (Cleveland), Dan Altavilla, Omaha (Kansas City), and Anthony Misiewicz, Louisville (Cincinnati). The three were on the Blaze in 2014, 2015 and 2016, respectively.

The Bakersfield Train Robbers baseball team swept a two-game weekend series at Sam Lynn Ballpark against the Austin Weirdos in Pecos League play. Bakersfield won 8-3 on Friday and then 17-9 on Saturday.

In Friday’s game, the Weirdos scored three runs in the second inning for its only lead in the game. The Train Robbers countered and took the lead for good in the fourth inning. Brock Slikker reached base on a fielder’s choice, enabling one run to score. Zach Beatty reached first on an error, getting another run across. When Beatty stole second, the catcher’s throw was errant and yet another runner scored for a 4-3 lead. Macs Carrillo then singled to drive in Beatty. In the fifth inning, Beaty drove in two runs with a single and Maxim Fullerton added another RBI single in the sixth.

Slikker, who was the starting pitcher for Bakersfield, went 5 1/3 innings and struck out six to even his season record to 3-3.

The Train Robbers offense was on full display on Saturday, namely Fullerton and Joe Riddle. Fullerton drove in seven runs and Riddle added four more against Austin.

It was 6-0 after the first inning as Riddle had an RBI single, Cade Fujii had a RBI single and a few batters later, Fullerton hit a grand slam. Austin got a few runs back in the third, but Riddle had a two-run single in the fourth inning. Austin did get the score to within 10-7 with a three-run homer by Cono Casale in the sixth, but Fullerton had a pair of RBI doubles in consecutive innings and Riddle had a sacrifice fly. Fullerton’s final run-scoring play was a fielder’s choice in the eighth.

While starter Levi Tucker and Brenden Poindexter each got roughed up a bit early, Lucas Belcher (3-0) got the win with two innings of scoreless relief.

The Train Robbers, who are 20-7 at home this season and 26-15-1 overall, started a three-game home series with Dublin on Monday. The teams play at 7:45 p.m. on Tuesday and Wednesday. These games will close out Bakersfield’s regular-season home schedule. The team will be on the road for games this Friday at Dublin and Saturday at Martinez, both starting at 6 p.m. Then they will begin 2 p.m. Sunday at Dublin. The playoffs start Monday.

The start of the regular season is less than a month away, but the CSUB women’s soccer team will be playing a Blue vs. White scrimmage game at 7 p.m. Saturday at the CSUB soccer field.

It will be the first opportunity to see the 2026 team, which is now directed by interim head coach Martin Navarro Jr. He is no stranger to the program. This will be his fifth year as Navarro has been with the team since 2022 when he began his coaching career as a graduate assistant coach. He was promoted in summer 2023 as an assistant coach and goalkeeper coach and became associate head coach in January. He was named interim head coach in March.

The Roadrunners open their 2026 season on the road, 6 p.m. Aug. 13 against the University of San Francisco. CSUB’s home opener is 11 a.m. Aug. 23 against Idaho State.

title: Why Astros don't plan to be sellers at MLB trade deadline
description: Houston may have a few movable pieces, but they likely aren't going anywhere.
fullText:
Why Astros don't plan to be sellers at MLB trade deadline originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Houston Astros are stuck in the middle.

Stuck between a postseason contender and a trade deadline seller.

Houston's problem starts with the contracts of its general manager, Dana Brown, and manager Joe Espada.

Both are in the final year of their agreements with the AL West organization. That complicates the future of shortstop Jeremy Pena and other potential trade chips on the roster.

"General manager Dana Brown has insisted the team will be buyers, but he is working in the final year of his contract. So is manager Joe Espada," The Athletic's Chandler Rome wrote. "Both men must save face and try to save themselves, so saying anything to the contrary is illogical, especially if they hope to keep this clubhouse intact."

According to Rome, the Astros asked right-hander Lance McCullers Jr. to waive his no-trade clause to free payroll in preparation for the deadline. McCullers was subsequently traded to the Milwaukee Brewers.

MORE: Dodgers' Shohei Ohtani injury update essentially ends Cy Young chances

title: Savannah Bananas Breakout Star Offers 3-Word Response On Sudden All-Star Health Scare
description: The former Savannah Bananas outfielder opened up about a scary medical situation that overshadowed his MLB All-Star accomplishment.
fullText:
The Chicago White Sox are entering the second half of the season in a surprisingly competitive playoff position amid the wide-open American League.

And one of the organization's biggest unexpected bright spots has been the emergence of first-time All-Star Tristan Peters. Peters was selected to the AL roster as a replacement for Nick Kurtz and deservedly so, as he is batting .301 with 75 hits on the year so far.

But perhaps the most intriguing thing about Peters’ rise for many fans is the fact that he used to play for the Savannah Bananas, which has lately captured the nation as an entertaining mix of baseball and on-field antics.

But as Peters prepared to enjoy the biggest week of his baseball career, his family's focus suddenly shifted away from the field after an unexpected medical scare involving his wife.

FORBES | By Peter Chawaga
Cubs’ Former Southpaw Walks Away From NL Powerhouse After 3-Game Debacle

The latest twist in Peters’ unlikely rise unfolded just before Major League Baseball's All-Star festivities officially began in Philadelphia.

As Peters was watching star teammate Munetaka Murakami practice, he received a message that his wife, Erin, was unable to get out of bed. He quickly returned to their hotel room and realized they would need to rush to the hospital.

"They called for help, and the next thing they knew they were in a local hospital with Erin undergoing CAT scans, trying to diagnose what was wrong,” Bob Nightengale reported for USA Today. “They spent the night in the hospital, taking turns watching the baby, with each getting about three hours apiece until leaving at 6 a.m. They went back to the hotel, and Erin's back felt just barely good enough to walk the All-Star Game Red Carpet with their baby, along with the other All-Stars."

In the immediate aftermath of the scare, Peters wasn’t sure how Erin’s health scare might develop. But the experience certainly turned what should have been a celebratory weekend into an emotional balancing act between family and baseball.

And after Erin encouraged him to participate in the game despite her pain, Peters sent a three-word message.

“She’s so amazing,” he said, per Nightengale, after she convinced him to participate despite her pain.

FORBES | By Peter Chawaga
Cardinals Lose Veteran Southpaw After 1-Day Stint

Peters' appearance at the All-Star Game represented one of the most unlikely journeys in baseball.

Before becoming a breakout major leaguer, he briefly spent time with the Savannah Bananas, though his stint came before the organization became a nationwide phenomenon dedicated to constant on-field clownery.

"Peters, a seventh-round pick out of Southern Illinois, had only four games of major-league experience before this season and was perhaps best known for briefly playing for the Savannah Bananas in 2021, before the (Milwaukee) Brewers drafted him in the seventh round that year,” Jon Greenberg noted for The Athletic. “But no, he wasn't dancing or playing on stilts."

Instead, Peters used that opportunity as a stepping stone toward professional baseball, eventually climbing through the minor leagues before earning his breakout season with the White Sox.

Now, what might have been remembered solely as his first All-Star experience following the Savannah Bananas tenure will also be remembered for the perspective he displayed while navigating a frightening family health emergency.

title: MLB Wants Coaches, Not Chatbots, Calling the Shots

fullText:
Major League Baseball has banned teams from using dugout iPads to run AI-powered tools that generate in-game strategy recommendations, marking a mid-season policy change aimed directly at custom apps that push tablets beyond review and reference work. Tablet use has become a familiar part of modern baseball broadcasts, with players and staff regularly reviewing information in the dugout. Regular viewers have grown accustomed to seeing teams huddled around devices, typically with the expectation that those tablets support performance review or last-minute statistical work. The league's concern is different. MLB officials intervened after teams reportedly began using hardware for generative AI tools and custom applications that crossed into decision-making territory. The policy change cuts off that use before it becomes a standard part of in-game management. The Athletic reported, that the commissioner's office delivered the news in a June 11 memo. Sources told The Athletic that as many as a third of MLB teams had used tablets for these unintended purposes. No clubs will face punishment. MLB review determined all organizations were compliant with the new rules. MLB's move fits into a longer tightening of in-game technology rules. iPad use during games faced increased restrictions after a sign-stealing scandal surfaced in 2021. In the years after that, teams pushed for more lenience, but the commissioner's office is now pulling back.

Baseball teams already pursue every legal informational edge, and fast data processing sits naturally inside the sport's modern analytics culture. But MLB is now separating analysis from automated tactical direction, especially when those recommendations could affect substitutions, pitch calls, and other live competitive decisions. The ban does not reject technology outright. Baseball is well suited to statistical analysis, and AI is effective at processing large volumes of data quickly. The issue is where that processing turns into live instruction. Baseball decisions are not made from numbers alone. Mental, and emotional performance can complicate the mathematically optimal answer at any given moment. MLB's new restriction preserves room for players and coaches to make those calls rather than allowing generative AI tools to become dugout decision engines. The report also contrasts this kind of AI use with technology that acts as a backup, including the new ABS system. That distinction matters. MLB is not moving away from tech-assisted baseball; it is drawing a boundary around tools that replace strategic judgment during games. For a league built on both data and instinct, the message is direct. Tablets can remain part of the dugout workflow, but AI-generated strategy calls are out.

title: MLB trade deadline watch: These five franchises could hold all the cards
description: With buyers outnumbering sellers, these five teams could have the biggest impact on MLB's trade deadline landscape.
fullText:
CHICAGO — Major League Baseball’s trade deadline doesn’t arrive for another 2½ weeks, but here we are as the second half of the regular season begins, and we can already tell you the winners of the trade deadline.

There are 23 teams still in first place or within four games of the wild-card race, meaning that there are just seven teams who plan to even moderately sell, with only the New York Mets and San Francisco Giants willing to do a complete fire sale.

In the words of one general manager: "If you’re going to have a bad year, this is the year to have it. It’s going to be a huge seller’s market unless things really shake out here in the next couple of weeks."

These days, the playoff race is in such flux that a team can be sellers one week, and buyers the next.

More MLB trade deadline: Ranking the best trade targets for contenders

Just look at the Boston Red Sox, who wallowed in mediocrity for three months, prepared to unload their high-priced veterans, only to go on a record-setting heater for two weeks, and now – at just half a game back in the wild-card race – should become buyers.

The San Diego Padres looked like they could be a formidable threat to the Los Angeles Dodgers, and now after the past month are talking about unloading All-Star closer Mason Miller and putting their high-priced stars on the market.

Who would imagine that these next 2½ weeks would not only decide the fate of two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, but perhaps the direction of 10 teams currently sitting outside of a playoff spot if the season ended today – but still within four games of a wild-card berth?

Here are the five most intriguing five teams to watch at the Aug. 3 trade deadline:

The Tigers weren’t listening to any offers when they were in the process of losing 21 of 25 games, but they were preparing to have their scouts scour the minor leagues to see what prospects they desired in any trade package for Tarik Skubal.

They were 22-38 and 11½ games back with Skubal on the injured list on June 1, but they have since taken off with Skubal returning. They are now 6½ games out of first place and, more important, just 3½ games out of a wild-card berth. They also have a healthy rotation, which produced a 3.48 ERA, fourth-best in MLB at the All-Star break, while yielding the third-lowest batting average.

They badly need bullpen help after blowing 19 saves, the second-most in baseball, but if they find a late reliever or two and grab another right-handed bat, why should the Tigers punt in a season with a franchise-record payroll just to get some pieces for the future?

Sure, trading Skubal will fortify their farm system, but it will also crush the morale in the clubhouse and infuriate their passionate fan base.

Besides, the American League is completely wide open. Just get into the dance, and you can be the last one standing in October.

And stop with the nonsense that the Tigers could thread the needle by trading Skubal and still adding pieces.

Trading Skubal, plain and simple, is surrendering.

Skubal could be the difference between a mesmerizing trade deadline and an awfully dull one.

And now they’re ready to blow it up.

You need a three-time batting champion? Second baseman Luis Arraez, who also has turned into a Gold Glove-caliber second baseman, can be yours.

You want a former Cy Young winner who can pitch under intense pressure and fortify any rotation? Ask for left-hander Robbie Ray.

You got $100 million or more to spare? Ask for third baseman Matt Chapman, shortstop Willy Adames or first baseman Rafael Devers, and they can be all yours.

They’re all ears, too, if someone wants to engage in serious talks about outfielder Jung-Hoo Lee.

Hey, when you’re 19½ games out of first place, with a 41-55 record, you’re listening to everything except Logan Webb, Casey Schmitt and Bryce Eldridge.

This is the West Coast version of the Giants, and yes, they’ve got plenty to sell, too.

They will trade veteran starter Freddy Peralta, reliever Luke Weaver, reliever Huascar Brazoban, and perhaps closer Devin Williams.

They will dump left-handed relievers Brooks Raley and A.J. Minter, right-hander Kodai Senga, and perhaps first baseman Mark Vientos, too.

And, don’t be surprised that if you ask for shortstop Francisco Lindor, who’s in the firth year of a 10-year, $341 million contract, David Stearns, president of baseball operations, stays on the phone listening.

Yes, Mets owner Steve Cohen did come out and say that Juan Soto and Lindor were staying put, but he also said that Stearns’s job is safe for two more years. And if Stearns didn’t want crowd favorite Pete Alonso around anymore, certainly he wouldn’t mind unloading Lindor’s contract.

Rival executives believe that Lindor will eventually be traded, but more likely in the offseason than now.

This is the team that everyone – well, at least outside the Friendly Confines at Wrigley Field – believes needs to be aggressive at the deadline.

They won 97 games last season and knocked off the Chicago Cubs in the National League division series, but they were rudely bounced out of the NLCS by the Los Angeles Dodgers before knowing what hit them.

They have the most electrifying starter in Jacob Misiorowski.

They’ve got a solid No. 2 starter in Kyle Harrison, who’s on the injured list but is soon expected to return.

They’ve got a lineup that doesn’t scare you, but they sure can irritate you.

Now, if they are ever going to get back into the World Series for the first time since 1982, this is the time.

They still have loving memories of what CC Sabathia did for them in 2008, going 11-2 with a 1.65 ERA in 17 starts, ending the Brewers’ postseason drought, which has now turned into seven playoff appearances in the past eight years.

They’ve got the second-best record in baseball this season at 59-37.

They’ve got the best farm system in baseball.

So, in the famous words of Theo Epstein when he acquired closer Aroldis Chapman for the Cubs in 2016 to take them to where they hadn't gone since 1908, "If not now, when?"

This is the year the Brewers should go all in.

Don’t work the margins and hope your $2.5 million gamble on Lance McCullers works.

Go get Skubal. If not Skubal, Robbie Ray. If not Ray, then Sonny Gray if he becomes available. Just go out and get reinforcements.

"From the outside looking in, or if you take just a purely analytical look at baseball, you don’t understand the impact that it has in the clubhouse," Epstein recently said on "The Lovable Reunion" podcast with Anthony Rizzo and David Ross. "These guys have done all their offseason work, grinded all of spring training, put the (guts) on the line the whole season. And then they look at the front office like, 'You guys have one (expletive) job. Get us what we need.'"

Let’s see if this is the year the Brewers put discipline aside for once and finally go all in.

One year, they’re trading away four prized prospects, including James Wood and CJ Abrams to acquire Washington Nationals outfielder Juan Soto.

One year, they’re trading away perhaps the finest prospect in baseball, shortstop Leo De Vries, for Athletics All-Star closer Mason Miller.

The next, they’re talking about trading him away.

The Padres, who recently sold for a stunning $3.9 billion, who sell out virtually every game they play, have looked like a discombobulated mess.

They are 48-48 and have no idea whether they should buy, go all in, sell, or go all-out.

They’re desperate for a starter, and without one, or even two, and a bounce-back second half from Manny Machado, they’re going nowhere and might as well sell.

But with A.J. Preller, MLB’s most aggressive wheeler and dealer, it’s anyone’s guess.

Follow Bob Nightengale on X: @Bnightengale

title: Yankees Predicted to Part Ways With $16 Million Infielder Amid Struggles
description: The New York Yankees could trade struggling third baseman Ryan McMahon, an MLB analyst suggested. The post Yankees Predicted to Part Ways With $16 Million Infielder Amid Struggles appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The New York Yankees have some holes to fill before the upcoming MLB trade deadline, but they could also make some subtractions to shore up their lineup.

The Yankees have a dire need for steady hitting to make up for the injured Aaron Judge, especially among their catchers. The team has already been linked to some hot trade targets, though its not yet clear just how aggressive the team will be in filling those needs.

The Yankees could do some strategic selling as well. Reporter Devon Platana of SI.com identified some Yankees players who could hit the trade block in the coming weeks, including an expensive infielder who has failed to produce much for the team.

Platana identified third baseman Ryan McMahon as one of the most likely trade pieces for the Yankees, along with shortstop Anthony Volpe. It could be more urgent for the Yankees to trade McMahon given the relatively large salary he carries.

“As mentioned earlier, the left side of the Yankees’ infield has left much to be desired,” Platana reported. “Volpe is only one half of the equation, though, as third baseman Ryan McMahon has been just as frustrating, if not more so, as he disappoints despite making $16 million annually.”

McMahon has struggled since joining the Yankees last season, hitting a low point this year as he is batting just .214 with a .655 OPS. Platana noted that his performance is “nothing short of underwhelming,” exacerbated by the fact that McMahon has the seventh-highest payroll on the team this season.

While he struggles at the plate, McMahon isn’t exactly offering relief on defense, Platana added.

“The Yankees should do whatever it takes to move on from McMahon and upgrade 3B, as he’s due to make another $16 million next season before becoming a free agent,” Platana wrote. “It’s better to turn the page now when, hopefully, a team will be desperate enough to roll the dice on the former All-Star, rather than losing him for nothing in 2027.”

Platana warned that the Yankees would not get much of a return for McMahon, but that shouldn’t hold them back from making a move if they find a willing trade partner.

“Even if a trade doesn’t yield the biggest return, trading McMahon away would be addition by subtraction, leaving Boone & Co. with one less headache to worry about,” Platana wrote.

McMahon could be used as a trade piece to help the Yankees land much-needed help elsewhere on the roster. MLB.com broke down the trade needs for each team, noting that the Yankees are in dire need of a catcher who can swing the bat.

“Entering the break, Yankees catchers ranked near the bottom of the league with a .176 batting average, .552 OPS and 46 wRC+,” the report noted. “While there are concerns about importing a catcher in-season because of potential disruption to the pitching staff, the Yankees have been strongly connected to the Twins’ Ryan Jeffers, who could comprise the right-handed-hitting part of a platoon with Austin Wells.”

title: What if MLB moved to a hard slot system?
description: Really, what if?
fullText:
No polemic or argument here — just a what if. You fill in the blanks.

The Rule 4 MLB Draft is weird. On its face, without any historical context, it’s just a way of adding younger players to organizations in a structured way. Worse teams pick before better teams, and it loops around until there are no players anyone wants to add left. However, because the players have to be treated at least perfunctorily as people and not as objects, they get financial incentive to join the organization, with players picked earlier getting more such incentive since the cost of not having them is relatively higher.

Except then we’ve got the history of the draft as collectively bargained and sometimes unilaterally set forth, where it’s become this crazy thing with bonus pools and strategies and penalties for going over (but not if you only go a little over) and contingency bonuses and participating in the MLB combine to avoid getting too lowball of an offer. Some of these things were natural, perhaps needed evolutions. Some are just complicated for their own sake.

So, given all that: what if there was just a hard slot system? Team takes a guy, guy’s bonus is immediately set at the slot for that pick. Want to pay less? Pass on a pick. Want to pay more? Well, you can’t, without doing stuff that’s not allowed and possibly getting slapped on the wrist or worse by MLB. Guy doesn’t want to play for your organization for slot? Too bad for both of you: you lose the guy, the guy loses a payday and has to wait a year to get re-drafted by someone else. (Maybe this system would include more than a one-year signing ineligibility for players that avoid accepting the slot bonus.)

I’m not going to speculate much in the body, but I do think that if this went into place in a vacuum, the real action would be on all the interaction effects. If the Rule 4 Draft had hard slots, what would teams do in International Amateur Free Agency as a pivot? Would there be more focus on developing undrafted guys? You’d probably see fewer high schoolers taken overall, which might change the developmental role of college programs, and the structure of minor league programs, since they’d have fewer raw high schoolers other than the elite guys… but maybe more younger IFA signees to make up the difference.

I will note that any hard slot system will probably be part of an MLB attempt to lower the cost of the draft and/or amateur talent acquisition overall. But, it doesn’t have to: there’s no reason why MLB can’t pair a hard slot proposal with a vast expansion of the slot per pick.

title: Chris Stapleton And MLB Toast Baseball's First League-Wide Cocktail
description: MLB has spent years building local food and beverage partnerships. Its first signature cocktail with Chris Stapleton’s Traveller Whiskey takes that strategy nationwide.
fullText:
For years, Major League Baseball (MLB) clubs have used food and beverage to reflect the personalities of their cities. At Fenway Park, Samuel Adams has become synonymous with the Red Sox experience through a long-running partnership rooted in Boston pride, while Yankee Stadium once embraced local brewer Blue Point, even introducing the exclusive Pinstripe Pilsner brewed specifically for the ballpark. Even bigger, the Mets have teamed with Korbel on a recent ‘Metsmosa’ offering. But none of this is new; ballparks across the country have increasingly highlighted hometown breweries, wineries and distilleries alongside regional culinary specialties.

Those partnerships have helped individual clubs deepen connections with local fans, turning concessions into an extension of each city's identity. However, this year, the MLB is taking a different approach.

Rather than creating another team-specific offering, the league is introducing its first official signature cocktail—one designed to be recognized whether fans are watching a game in New York, Los Angeles or St. Louis. In doing so, MLB is moving beyond localized beverage partnerships toward creating a shared experience that belongs to the league itself. The league recently debuted The Rally Cap, a whiskey cocktail created in partnership with Traveller Whiskey, Chris Stapleton’s whiskey brand made in conjunction with Buffalo Trace. The sipper is made with Traveller Whiskey, lemonade and iced tea and is now available in stadiums across the U.S.

The launch is about more than adding another beverage to the menu. As ballparks continue to evolve into all-day entertainment destinations with elevated food and beverage programs, MLB sees an opportunity to create another shared experience for fans—one that can be enjoyed at the stadium and recreated at home.

"From a marketing perspective, we like showcasing baseball as a lifestyle for fans as much as it is a sport," says Uzma Rawn Dowler, MLB's CMO and senior vice president of global corporate partnerships. "In working with Traveller Whiskey, we saw an opportunity to create a unique beverage that could elevate the gameday experience while piquing the curiosity of new fans and deepening the engagement of existing ones."

Food and beverage have become an important part in the evolution of the ballpark, giving fans additional ways to connect with their favorite teams beyond the action on the field. While local partnerships remain an important part of each club’s identity, The Rally Cap represents one of the first attempts to create a beverage that belongs to MLB as a whole rather than to any single franchise.

According to Dowler, the concept wasn’t the result of years of planning but grew naturally from MLB’s relationship with Traveller Whiskey, which became the league’s first Official Whiskey last year. It led the hospitality team to recognize an opportunity to allow fans to enjoy a treat at the ballpark and then recreate that experience at home; no matter what game they’re watching at what time of the year.

The drink itself was intentionally designed to feel familiar. Lemonade and iced tea evoke summer afternoons at the ballpark, while Traveller Whiskey gives the cocktail an approachable foundation that fans can easily concoct at home.

For Stapleton, whose touring schedule has turned visits to Major League ballparks into a personal tradition, the collaboration was a natural fit.

"Whenever we’re out on the road, wherever it’s possible, we go to baseball games," Stapleton says. "Seeing the stadiums and experiencing each team’s unique baseball culture has become one of my favorite ways to get to know the identities of the people and cities they’re in. Needless to say, I was thrilled last year when Traveller Whiskey became the first official whiskey of [the MLB] and now we're just as excited to announce 'The Rally Cap.'"

Down to his final out, Walker could keep swinging as long as the magenta ball went over the fence. Any non-home run would start a re-coronation of Schwarber, already Philadelphia's home run king as MLB's current regular-season leader with 32.

title: MLB All-Star Byron Buxton gives very direct answer about waiving his no trade clause
description: As the MLB trade deadline draws closer, Minnesota Twins star Byron Buxton has become one of the more intriguing names mentioned in trade rumors. Despite the speculation, Buxton doesn’t appear interested in going anywhere. The veteran outfielder recently gave a…
fullText:
As the MLB trade deadline draws closer, Minnesota Twins star Byron Buxton has become one of the more intriguing names mentioned in trade rumors. Despite the speculation, Buxton doesn’t appear interested in going anywhere. The veteran outfielder recently gave a blunt response when asked whether he would consider waiving his no-trade clause if a contender, such as the Philadelphia Phillies, attempted to acquire him. His answer couldn’t have been clearer: “I ain’t going nowhere.”

MORE: MLB Power Rankings: All 30 teams ranked ahead of the 2026 All-Star Game

Trade speculation has followed Buxton for much of the season, largely because of his talent and the number of contenders searching for impact players ahead of the deadline.

The Phillies have frequently been mentioned as a potential landing spot, but they’re far from the only team that could benefit from adding an All-Star caliber center fielder.

The New York Yankees, Houston Astros, Cleveland Guardians, and Atlanta Braves have also been connected to Buxton as clubs that could use another difference-maker for the stretch run. Based on his comments, though, those teams may be wasting their time.

Minnesota has little reason to give up on the season. Although Buxton is currently on the injured list, he’s expected to return sometime in July. More importantly, the Twins remain firmly in the playoff hunt.

They enter the second half just three games behind in the American League Central while also sitting tied with the Seattle Mariners for the final AL Wild Card spot. Those standings make it difficult to justify moving one of the franchise’s cornerstone players.

Buxton’s response speaks volumes about where his priorities are. Rather than entertaining the possibility of joining another contender, the Twins’ star made it clear that he wants to remain in Minnesota and help the organization reach the postseason.

That’s welcome news for Twins fans, who know how valuable Buxton can be when healthy. Trade rumors are likely to continue until the deadline passes, especially given the number of contenders looking to upgrade their outfield.

But unless something dramatically changes over the next few weeks, Buxton has made his stance crystal clear. As far as he’s concerned, his future remains exactly where it is now—with the Minnesota Twins.

title: Jordan Walker Makes History That Mark McGuire, Albert Pujols Never hit
description: Jordan Walker hit notable history in his MLB All-Star Game Home Run Derby win. The post Jordan Walker Makes History That Mark McGuire, Albert Pujols Never hit appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Jordan Walker entered Citizens Bank Park surrounded by Philadelphia Phillies colors. The St. Louis Cardinals representative later overheard Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper plastered as the proverbial favorites in the 2026 Home Run Derby. Then Walker faced long comeback odds to topple the former.

But Walker delivered an epic derby comeback for the ages. Pulling off the stunning upset against the heavy favorite Schwarber by completing the final six swings of the finals.

Walker’s night started to align his way the moment he beat out Harper for the semifinals spot. He then became all smiles in accepting the two-bats trophy and derby chain.

And he hit a mark that franchise legends Mark McGuire and Albert Pujols never hit before.

McGuire is known for delivering power hits during his late 1990s Cardinals run. Pujols carried that momentum in his illustrious career during the 2000s.

But Walker hits this stunning milestone: He’s the first Cardinals player to ever win the Home Run Derby crown.

Even McGuire never won the 1998 derby during his widely-viewed home run duel with Sammy Sosa, when both went after the single-season HR record. Seattle Mariners star Ken Griffey Jr. took the derby championship in that all-star event at Coors Field in Denver.

Pujols participated in the renown event five times: 2003, 2007, 2009, 2015 and his final one of 2022. The ’03 derby emerged as the closest he ever got to winning the event, eventually losing out to Garrett Anderson of the Anaheim Angels.

The right-handed batter hit more than franchise history, though.

Walker delivered another historic milestone, per OPTAstats after the derby concluded.

“Jordan Walker is the first non-rookie to win the Home Run Derby after never having hit at least 20 HR in a season entering the year they won the derby,” the account posted on the social media website X, formerly known as Twitter.

Which now shows that even the MLB leader in home runs are no longer guaranteed to be the odds on favorite to win the event. MLB analyst Sarah Langs dropped another history nugget now attached to Walker: fifth-youngest winner.

The 1993 victor Juan Gonzalez remains the youngest derby winner ever. Gonzalez claimed his title while with the Texas Rangers.

National analysts even outside of baseball took to social media in reacting to the 2026 winner.

Longtime ESPN personality Kevin Negandhi praised how calm Walker became.

“Impressive performance from Jordan Walker. Perfect example of staying cool the entire time and being in control,” Negandhi said on X.

Even fellow ESPN personality but renown college football analyst Kirk Herbstreit raved about Walker.

Jordan Walker is a STUD!!!!!Congratulations young fella!!!His parents reactions were perfect. @Cardinals

— Kirk Herbstreit (@KirkHerbstreit) July 14, 2026

Walker even hit a massive payday too. His current Cardinals contract doesn’t pay him in the millions, which sits at $799,400 currently. But he earns $1 million in taking home the the derby trophy.

He felt unfazed by the boos too, as he faced the sea of red representing loud and boisterous Phillies fans. Walker entered as the underdog and came out making new history.

title: How is Ben Rice doing at MLB Home Run Derby? See live updates
description: At Philadelphia's Citizens Bank Park, Yankees' slugger Ben Rice, a first-time All-Star, is at the Home Run Derby. See how he's doing.
fullText:
Ben Rice's dream has come true.

The New York Yankees' first-time All-Star is participating in Monday night's MLB Home Run Derby, taking his cuts with some of the league's biggest sluggers at Citizens Bank Park in Philadelphia, home of the Phillies.

Hours before the Derby began, Rice was named the AL's Player of the Week, batting .423 (11-for-26) with five home runs, 12 RBI and a 1.577 OPS, as the Yanks moved into the break on a four-game winning streak.

Here's what to know about Rice as he participates in the Home Run Derby:

Rice, who is 27, has been with the Yankees organization for five years since being drafted in the 12th round of the 2021 MLB Draft. He made his big-league debut with the Yankees in June 2024.

For the season, Rice is batting .279 with 29 homers, 68 RBI and a .971 OPS in 91 games, serving as both a designated hitter and first baseman. This is his first All-Star selection.

Last week, Rice officially announced his Home Run Derby entry on social media, with an accompanying video from about 22 years ago.

It showed a very young Ben Rice, wearing a Yankees jersey, taking big swings against his dad.

Dan Rice was a college pitcher at Brown (his son would attend Dartmouth) and it’s “always been a dream of ours," Ben Rice said, to participate in the Home Run Derby.

In the offseason, Dan Rice still pitches to his son, who learned how to hit breaking stuff by facing his dad’s signature curveball.

During a recent Yankees team flight, Rice watched some of Aaron Judge’s Home Run Derby appearances with the captain, who won it in 2017.

Cody Bellinger has also been a past Home Run Derby participant, and fellow Yankees All-Star teammate Cam Schlittler pledged to be Rice’s go-to guy for Gatorade breaks.

Mostly, “I just want to enjoy it, have fun taking BP with my dad on a big-league field in front of a bunch of people,’’ Rice said recently.

title: UConn lefty Charlie West picked in seventh round of MLB Draft by Los Angeles Dodgers
description: The Friday night starter for the Huskies was the lone UConn player picked in this weekend’s draft.
fullText:
A UConn Husky heard his name called on the second day of the 2026 MLB Draft. Left-handed pitcher Charlie West was selected in the seventh round with the No. 223 overall pick by the Los Angeles Dodgers. The South Setauket, New York, native pitched the past three seasons in Storrs.

West had a great spring for the Huskies, receiving All-Big East First Team honors after he led the conference in strikeouts with 111. He made 16 starts and had a 4.12 ERA in 87.1 innings, accumulating a 6-6 record on the mound. His best performance of the season came on April 12 when he struck out a career-high 14 batters against Butler.

The selection marks 21-straight MLB Drafts in which UConn has had at least one player drafted or signed by an MLB club. West is the 80th player selected under head coach Jim Penders, who has had a player drafted or signed in all but one of his 23 years leading the dugout in Storrs.

West will try and join the group of 10 other players who have made the big leagues in Penders’ tenure, most recently Kyler Fedko with the Minnesota Twins earlier this year. West is the 18th Husky to be picked in the first 10 rounds since 2009.

So far this summer, West has a 2.16 ERA in four starts for the Brewster Whitecaps in the Cape Cod League, striking out 26 batters in 16.2 innings entering Monday.

Former Husky pitcher Ben Casparius is currently in the Dodgers organization as well and is currently on the 60-day injured list with a shoulder injury.
